description_en: Sparse annual vegetation on the drift line of sandy and shingle beaches, where stranded seaweed and other organic debris raise the nitrogen content of the substrate. Dominant is Cakile maritima, joined by Salsola kali and Atriplex species and, further south, Glaucium flavum and Euphorbia peplis; Mediterranean shores add Matthiola sinuata and Eryngium maritimum, the Black Sea coast Argusia sibirica. The stand occupies the uppermost, most mobile part of the beach, subject to occasional inundation by storm tides and constant sand movement, from the Baltic to the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Composition shifts with region and with the amount and type of drift material rather than with soil in the usual sense. The vegetation is annual and pioneer by nature, renewed each year on shifting ground and destroyed by beach cleaning, trampling and coastal engineering as readily as by storms. It lies seaward of the perennial vegetation of stony banks (1220) and of the embryonic dunes of 2110.

Perennial vegetation of the upper shingle beach, dominated by Crambe maritima and Honckenya peploides, with Leymus arenarius on Baltic shingle, Lathyrus japonicus on Channel shores and Crithmum maritimum on Atlantic coasts further south. Stands sit above the drift line proper, on coarse, well drained shingle largely free of fine sediment, from the Baltic through the Channel to the Atlantic seaboard. Named associations vary regionally: Elymo-Crambetum on Baltic shingle, Lathyro-Crambetum along the Channel, Crithmo-Crambetum on Atlantic shores. On more stable, mature shingle further inland from the upper beach, grassland, heath and scrub can develop, and unusual lichen and bryophyte dominated stands occur on the oldest surfaces. The type depends on shingle structures large and stable enough to escape regular wave disturbance; trampling and extraction of shingle destroy it readily. It differs from the annual drift line vegetation of 1210 by its perennial, more established cover on coarser, more stable material.

Vegetated rock cliffs with their crevices, ledges and cliff tops along the Atlantic and Baltic coasts, exposed bedrock whose zonation reflects distance from salt spray. Nearest the sea, crevice and ledge communities of the Crithmo-Armerietalia hold Crithmum maritimum, Armeria maritima and Spergularia rupicola; further up, where soil is deeper, closed maritime grassland of the Silenion maritimae carries Silene uniflora, Plantago coronopus and Festuca rubra. Further inland or on sheltered cliffs this passes into maritime heath, calcareous or acid grassland, tall herb and scrub vegetation enriched with coastal species; soft, actively eroding coasts show a shifting mosaic instead of clear zonation. Composition varies with exposure, geology, region and the guano input of nesting seabirds. Management is light, mainly grazing on cliff top grassland; the chief threats are recreation, cliff stabilisation and coastal development. Loamy or sandy soft cliffs, less steep and less stable, are treated as a separate type though sharing much of the same flora.

Vegetated cliffs and rocky shores of the Mediterranean, adjoining Atlantic coasts of southwestern Iberia and, locally, the Black Sea, assigned to the Crithmo-Limonietalia. Crithmum maritimum forms the constant element, joined by numerous, often very locally endemic Limonium species together with Armeria, Euphorbia, Daucus and Asteriscus maritimus. Stands occupy crevices, ledges and cliff tops exposed to salt spray, with zonation and species composition governed by exposure, bedrock and regional climate; many Limonium taxa are confined to a single cliff system, giving the type an unusually fine grained endemism. Soft, eroding cliffs of clay, shale or sand nearby carry a related but distinct, poorly studied assemblage treated apart from the hard rock cliffs described here. Threats are chiefly recreational pressure and coastal development on the narrow, linear stands, which cannot retreat once the cliff base is altered. It parallels the Atlantic and Baltic cliffs of 1230 but is set apart by its markedly higher endemic Limonium diversity.

Vegetated basalt sea cliffs of the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores, narrow strips of rock shaped by salt spray and carrying a flora rich in island endemics. On the Canaries and Madeira the Frankenio-Astydamietalia dominate, with Astydamia latifolia, Limonium pectinatum, Frankenia ericifolia, Schizogyne sericea and Argyranthemum frutescens; on the Azores the Festucion petraeae is built around the endemic Festuca petraea alongside Azorina vidalii and Euphorbia azorica. Zonation of crevice and ledge vegetation differs between the three archipelagos, reflecting their separate volcanic geology and biogeographic history, and nesting seabirds add a nutrient-rich, guano-fed element near colonies. The habitat occupies the same cliff position as 1230 and 1240 further north and east, but is distinguished by its wholly Macaronesian endemic flora with no equivalent on the continental coasts. Isolation on small islands makes individual stands vulnerable to any single disturbance, from coastal development to introduced herbivores.

Open annual vegetation of periodically flooded mud and sand, dominated by succulent Chenopodiaceae, chiefly Salicornia species and Suaeda maritima, sometimes with Salsola. It occurs on both coastal salt marshes and inland salt basins across Europe, in several regional forms: glasswort swards of the Thero-Salicornietalia on tidal coastal mud; Mediterranean halo-nitrophilous pioneer stands of the Frankenion pulverulentae with Frankenia pulverulenta and Cressa cretica; Atlantic pearlwort communities of the Saginion maritimae with Sagina maritima at the dune to marsh transition; and, from Pannonia to the Far East, sparse Crypsis stands on drying solonchak mud. All forms share a strict dependence on alternating inundation and desiccation with surface salt efflorescence; woody or perennial encroachment signals a shift away from this regime, usually through reduced flooding or drainage. Diagnostic species and syntaxa differ sharply by region, so identification rests on the dominant annual chenopod and the local hydrology rather than on a single indicator species.

Non-coastal salt vegetation formed around zones of saline seepage, springs and streams and stagnant brackish water, with halophilous swards and fringing reed beds at the margins of the brackish water bodies. Characteristic plants are Aster tripolium, Puccinellia distans, Juncus gerardii, Plantago maritima, Triglochin maritima, Spergularia salina and Salicornia species, with Elymus atherica and Halimione pedunculata locally. The habitat forms where salt reaches the surface through geological seepage rather than tidal action, so it is always small and scattered, embedded in a matrix of ordinary inland vegetation. Artificial or semi-natural sites, such as old salt workings, are included only where natural stands no longer exist regionally or where they hold an Annex II species. Any disruption of the saline seepage, whether by drainage, dilution with fresh water or infilling, removes the halophilous flora within a few seasons and cannot be reversed by management alone. It is distinguished from the Pannonic salt steppes of 1530 by its scattered, non-steppic, seepage-fed occurrence.

Perennial coastal scrub of nitrophilous, salt-tolerant shrubs on dry soils under an arid to semi-arid Mediterranean climate, assigned to the Pegano-Salsoletea. Salsola vermiculata, Artemisia herba-alba, Lycium intricatum and Atriplex halimus form the woody framework, with Suaeda and Camphorosma species adding further salt tolerant elements; stands range from low and open to, in places, taller and denser. The habitat concentrates on disturbed ground near the coast, where sea-borne salt and, close to seabird colonies, guano keep soil nutrient and salt levels high; outliers extend into Macaronesia beyond the Mediterranean proper. Composition and structure vary considerably with disturbance and local salt input, from sparse chamaephyte cover to closed matorral. Because it establishes readily on disturbed, nutrient and salt enriched ground, it can expand where natural vegetation has been cleared, which makes its boundary with ordinary ruderal or halophile scrub a matter of species combination rather than physiognomy alone.

Perennial salt vegetation of Mediterranean coasts and Iberian inland salt basins, built from rosette forming Limonium species or, on more open ground, from tussocks of esparto grass, Lygeum spartum, assigned to the Limonietalia. Soils are permeated, though not permanently flooded, by saline water and dry out completely in summer with a surface crust of salt efflorescence; associated stands of the Arthrocnemetalia, Thero-Salicornietalia and Saginetalia maritimae fill the wetter and more disturbed microsites within the same mosaic. Halopeplis amplexicaulis, Microcnemion coralloides, Senecio auricula and Sphenopus divaricatus complete the diagnostic flora. Regional syntaxa are numerous and often confined to a single Iberian basin or short coastal stretch, reflecting the strict local control of hydrology and salinity on species composition. The type occupies the same extreme, seasonally desiccating salt habitats as continental salt steppes elsewhere, from which it is set apart mainly by its distinctive Limonium and Lygeum dominated syntaxa rather than by site conditions.

Open garrigue of the Iberian peninsula on gypsum rich soils, physiognomically a low chamaephyte scrub with a lichen crust and a flush of spring annuals after rain. Gypsophilous specialists dominate: Gypsophila hispanica, G. struthium, Helianthemum squamatum, Herniaria fruticosa, Lepidium subulatum and Ononis tridentata, with thymes, germanders, rockroses and composites such as Centaurea and Jurinea filling out the community. The type is tied to gypsum outcrops under a dry to semi-arid Mediterranean climate and is largely confined to central and eastern Spain, following the syntaxa Lepidion subulati, Gypsophilion hispanicae and Thymo-Teucrion verticillati. Extreme edaphic and climatic conditions keep the vegetation open and stable over long periods, and it tolerates light grazing; the chief threats are gypsum quarrying and conversion to arable or irrigated land, which destroy the substrate itself rather than merely the vegetation. The gypsum substrate and narrow endemic flora separate it from ordinary calcareous garrigue at a glance.

Halophytic vegetation of the Pannonian and Ponto-Sarmatic lowlands, formed under a continental climate with hot, arid summers that draw salt to the surface through evaporation from shallow groundwater. The type spans dry salt pans and steppes, humid salt meadows and the zoned annual vegetation of periodically flooded salt lakes, with Artemisia santonicum, Puccinellia species, Camphorosma annua, Festuca pseudovina and Plantago tenuiflora among the dominants, and Juncus gerardii, Aster tripolium and Carex distans in the wetter zones. Much of the vegetation is of natural origin but has long been shaped by extensive cattle grazing, which keeps the sward open and prevents encroachment by reed and scrub; abandonment of grazing as much as drainage threatens the type today. Zonation from dry steppe through salt meadow to the flooded lake margin is the diagnostic feature in the field, more reliable than any single species. It contrasts with the seepage-bound inland salt meadows of 1340 by its steppic, climatically driven salinity and its characteristic zoned mosaic around shallow salt lakes.

Vegetation of glaciofluvial islands in the Baltic archipelago, built from well sorted sand, gravel or till with scattered stones and boulders, and shaped by brackish water, ongoing post-glacial land upheaval and constant wind and sun exposure. Succession following land upheaval produces a mosaic of beach, heath and grassland stages in the same small area, with Calluna vulgaris, Empetrum nigrum and Juniperus communis on older, more developed ground and Honckenya peploides, Cakile maritima and Leymus arenarius on the youngest, most exposed shore. Bare bedrock and sparse pioneer stands are common, and bird guano locally raises nutrient input and species diversity. The habitat includes the adjoining sublittoral vegetation of algae such as Fucus vesiculosus and Chara aspera, and provides important nesting sites for seabirds and haul out sites for seals. It differs from the boreal Baltic sandy beaches of 1640 by its rocky, esker derived substrate and from the small islets of 1620 by its distinctly sorted glaciofluvial material rather than bare Precambrian bedrock.

Vegetation of skerries, islets and small rocky islands in the outer Baltic archipelago, built on Precambrian metamorphic bedrock, till or thin sediment, mostly treeless and often almost bare. Wind, salt spray, intense sunlight and ongoing land upheaval drive a sparse, mosaic like pioneer vegetation, with Sedum acre, Silene viscosa, Juniperus communis and Cochlearia danica among the characteristic plants and xerophytes and lichens prominent on the most exposed rock. Bird colonies raise local nutrient levels through guano, increasing species diversity around nesting sites, and shallow rockpools carry their own distinct aquatic flora and fauna. The surrounding sublittoral vegetation of algae such as Fucus vesiculosus and Furcellaria lumbricalis belongs to the same type. Land upheaval keeps the vegetation in permanent, slow succession rather than a stable end stage. It is distinguished from the esker islands of 1610 by its bare Precambrian bedrock in place of sorted glaciofluvial sand and gravel.

Perennial vegetation of sheltered to exposed sandy beaches on the Finnish and Swedish Baltic coast, gently sloping and shaped by wave action but far less by tides than Atlantic beaches, which favours a higher share of perennial species over annuals. Sand binding plants dominate, chiefly Ammophila arenaria, Leymus arenarius and Elytrigia juncea subsp. boreoatlantica, with Lathyrus japonicus subsp. maritimus, Honckenya peploides and Cakile maritima among the associates and occasional stones or boulders scattered through the sand. Large areas of bare sand persist nearest the shore, and drift belts of stranded organic matter along the upper beach support a conspicuous insect fauna. Baltic sand beaches of this kind are relatively uncommon and typically small, more restricted than equivalent Atlantic sand beaches. Grazing or trampling pressure is usually low given the remoteness of most sites, and the chief threat is direct physical disturbance of the shore. It differs from the Atlantic and Baltic sand beach type by its stronger cover of perennial sand binders relative to annual pioneers.

The earliest stage of dune formation, low ridges and hummocks of wind blown sand at the upper edge of the beach or as a narrow seaward fringe at the foot of taller dunes. On Atlantic and Baltic coasts the pioneers are Elymus farctus, Leymus arenarius and Honckenya peploides; further south, on Mediterranean and Black Sea shores, Sporobolus pungens, Otanthus maritimus, Medicago marina and Eryngium maritimum take their place. These grasses and creeping herbs trap sand carried up from the beach, building the low, still discontinuous ridges that either wash away in the next storm or develop further into the taller, more stable ridges of 2120. The vegetation cover is sparse and species poor, on sand still close to the strandline and largely free of humus. Because the embryonic ridges are the first line of natural coastal defence, trampling and beach cleaning at this stage prevent dune building altogether rather than merely damaging established vegetation. The type grades seaward into the annual drift line vegetation of 1210 and landward into the white dunes of 2120.

Mobile, still actively building dunes forming the seaward ridge or ridges of a dune system, dominated by Ammophila arenaria, whose deep, fast growing root system copes with continuous sand burial. On Atlantic and Baltic coasts it grows with Eryngium maritimum, Euphorbia paralias and Calystegia soldanella; on Mediterranean shores with Echinophora spinosa and Cutandia maritima; and on the Zygophyllion fontanesii of parts of the Mediterranean, distinct associates such as Zygophyllum fontanesii and the rare endemic Androcymbium psammophilum appear instead. The dunes remain mobile as long as sand supply continues, with the marram grass advancing upward through accumulating sand faster than it is buried. Cover is open with few species, on nutrient poor sand largely free of organic matter. Trampling breaches the marram cover and triggers blow outs that can destabilise the whole ridge. The type follows on from the embryonic dunes of 2110 and stabilises further inland into the fixed grey dunes of 2130 once sand supply slows.

Fixed, no longer mobile dunes stabilised by a closed cover of perennial grassland with abundant lichens and mosses, on Atlantic, Channel, North Sea, Baltic and Black Sea coasts. Northern stands of the Galio-Koelerion carry Corynephorus canescens and Festuca rubra with Tortula ruraliformis and Cladonia lichens; further south, dwarf shrub rich Biscay grey dunes of the Euphorbio-Helichrysion add Helichrysum stoechas and Artemisia campestris, and thermo-Atlantic stands of the Crucianellion maritimae are built around Crucianella maritima. Locally, dune grassland grades inland into calcicole Mesobromion swards or thermophilous Trifolio-Geranietea fringes with Geranium sanguineum, and sparse Thero-Airion swards occupy the most oligotrophic sand. Calcium content falls with dune age, driving succession toward acidic dune heath. Grazing or mowing has traditionally kept the sward open; abandonment allows scrub and woodland to close in, while trampling and nitrogen deposition favour coarse grasses over the lichen rich turf. It follows the mobile white dunes of 2120 once sand movement has ceased.

Low, dwarf-shrub heath on decalcified, fixed dune sand along the cooler Atlantic and Baltic coasts, dominated by Empetrum nigrum, often with Calluna vulgaris, growing on stabilised sands that have lost their original lime content through leaching. Occurs on dune ridges and in dune slacks, the latter with Erica tetralix accompanying or replacing Empetrum. Diagnostic species include Carex arenaria, Genista tinctoria, Pyrola rotundifolia, Salix repens and lichens such as Cladonia portentosa; mosses like Hypnum cupressiforme and Dicranum scoparium form a dense ground layer. The stand persists where wind exposure or light grazing keeps scrub and woodland from establishing; without such pressure it develops toward dune scrub or wooded dunes (2180). In Germany the type includes the strongly endangered Empetrum heathland of the Geest. Distinguished from the Atlantic Calluno-Ulicetea dunes of 2150 by the dominance of Empetrum over Calluna and gorse, and from dry sand heaths inland (2310, 2320) by its position on genuinely dune sand.

Heath of fixed, decalcified dune sand along the warmer, more humid Atlantic coasts of France, Belgium, Britain and Iberia, dominated by Calluna vulgaris together with Erica cinerea, E. ciliaris, E. scoparia or Ulex species, in Iberia largely built by the alliance Ericion umbellatae. The sward carries a strong contingent of grasses and sedges, including Carex arenaria and C. trinervis, and grows on stable, sharply draining sands that formed on formerly calcareous dune ridges. It is kept open by wind exposure and by light, extensive grazing; where these cease it passes into dune scrub or wooded dunes. Distinguished from the Empetrum-dominated dunes of 2140 further north by the dominance of Calluna and spiny legumes rather than Empetrum, and from inland heaths of 2310 by its dune setting and Atlantic species pool.

Sea-buckthorn (Hippophae rhamnoides) scrub forming as a stage of forest colonisation in both dry and humid dune depressions. The nitrogen-fixing shrub forms dense, often thorny thickets that stabilise the sand and enrich it, opening the way for later successional scrub and woodland. It occurs together with Carex arenaria on the open sand beneath and around the stands. As a colonising formation the type is transitional: on Atlantic and Baltic coasts it forms part of a broader scrub mosaic that also includes gorse and other shrub-dominated stands, and it typically gives way in time to broadleaved wooded dunes (2180) or other scrub types once the pioneer stage passes. In the field it is recognised simply by the dominance of Hippophae rhamnoides itself, easily told by its silvery, narrow leaves and orange berries.

Creeping willow (Salix repens subsp. argentea, syn. S. arenaria) communities of the Salicion arenariae, colonising wet dune slacks where the willow forms low, mat-like carpets over damp sand. As the water table falls or wind-blown sand accumulates, these stands develop either toward mesophilous communities with Pyrola rotundifolia, Viola canina and Monotropa hypopitys, toward drier Salix stands with Carlina vulgaris and Thalictrum minus, or toward Salix repens stands enriched with Mesobromion grassland elements. The type thus marks a hinge point in dune-slack succession rather than a fixed endpoint. Diagnostic beyond the willow itself is accompanying Hippophae rhamnoides and Carex arenaria on adjoining drier ground. Separated from the wetter dune-slack vegetation of 2190, where creeping willow also occurs but within fen, grassland or reedbed communities rather than as the structuring dominant.

Long-established natural or semi-natural forest of coastal dunes across the Atlantic, continental and boreal regions, with a well developed woodland structure and a full complement of woodland species rather than pioneer scrub. On acid dune sand it corresponds to oak and beech-oak groves with birch of the Quercion robori-petraeae, elsewhere to forests of the Quercetalia pubescenti-petraeae. Pioneer stages are open stands of Betula species and Crataegus monogyna, or mixed woodland with Fraxinus excelsior, Quercus robur, Ulmus minor and Acer pseudoplatanus; in wet dune slacks, pioneer Salix alba woodland develops into humid mixed or marsh forest. On the southern Atlantic coast the type is mainly mixed Pinus pinaster and Quercus ilex forest, or stands of Quercus suber, Q. robur or Q. pubescens; on Baltic coasts, pioneer forest of Alnus species or Pinus sylvestris. The species complement varies strongly with local site conditions. Separated from the open dune scrub of 2160 and 2260 by closed canopy and woodland understorey, and from inland forest of the same alliances by its position on stabilised coastal dune sand.

Complex of humid depressions within dune systems, among the richest and most specialised dune habitats and strongly threatened by any lowering of the water table. Five subtypes are distinguished by hydrology and vegetation: permanent dune-slack pools with freshwater aquatics such as Chara, Elodea, Hippuris and Potamogeton; pioneer swards of humid sand and pool margins with low salinity; calcareous, occasionally acidic fens often invaded by creeping willow (Salix repens); humid grasslands and rush beds, again often with creeping willow; and reedbeds, tall-sedge stands and canebeds. The mosaic runs from dwarf rush and bryophyte pioneer vegetation through wet grassland to mire, swamp and open water, and the water table fluctuates seasonally, less so around the Baltic. Distinguished from drier, stabilised dune grassland by standing wetness, and from the creeping-willow dominated dunes of 2170, where succession runs toward mesophilous or xerophilous stands rather than fen or open water.

Complex sandy coastal plain habitat of oceanic, cool and moist climates, largely confined to Ireland and Scotland, shaped partly by grazing and rotational cultivation. The wind-blown sand carries a significant share of shell-derived material, giving a lime-rich soil with pH usually above 7. Vegetation is herbaceous grassland with only scattered sand-binding species, including Festuca rubra, Galium verum, Lotus corniculatus, Plantago lanceolata, Poa pratensis and Trifolium repens, with locally occurring specialities such as Dactylorhiza fuchsii subsp. hebridensis and Euphrasia marshallii. The type sits within a wider mosaic of grey dune grassland and, in wetter hollows, dune slack vegetation, without being fully equivalent to either. Traditional low-intensity grazing and rotational cropping maintain the open sward; abandonment or agricultural intensification both threaten it. The priority form is restricted to Ireland.

Fixed dune grassland of the western and central Mediterranean, the Adriatic, the Ionian Sea and North Africa, characterised by Crucianella maritima and Pancratium maritimum on stabilised sand set back from the active foredune. The sward sits within a broader belt of Mediterranean and Macaronesian grey dune grassland, from which it is distinguished by the dominance of these two species and by syntaxa of the alliance Crucianellion maritimae, together with companions such as Medicago marina, Medicago littoralis, Elytrigia juncea, Lagurus ovatus and spring ephemerals like Vulpia fasciculata and Malcolmia ramosissima. It occupies a more stable, later successional position than the mobile foredune ahead of it, and gives way landward to Mediterranean dune scrub. Threatened throughout its range by tourism infrastructure, trampling and the spread of non-native species on Mediterranean coasts.

Coastal dune grassland of the Mediterranean characterised by Euphorbia terracina together with Ephedra distachya, Silene nicaeensis and S. subconica, on stabilised sands within the wider belt of Mediterranean and Macaronesian grey dune grassland. The type is set apart from neighbouring dune grasslands mainly by the presence and local dominance of Euphorbia terracina and its named companions rather than by a distinct structure; the sward is otherwise a graminoid and herb cover typical of fixed Mediterranean dunes, with spring ephemerals appearing after rain. It occupies a stable position in dune succession, later than the mobile foredune, and gives way to scrub once grazing or disturbance no longer keeps it open. Material for this type is sparse beyond its diagnostic species; distinguishing it in the field rests on their presence.

Sparse, short-lived grassland of deep sand in dry interdunal depressions along Mediterranean coasts, dominated by small annuals with an often abundant ephemeral spring bloom. Characteristic species are Malcolmia lacera, M. ramosissima, Evax asterisciflora, E. lusitanica, Anthyllis hamosa and Linaria pedunculata, the dune counterpart of the inland pseudo-steppe grasslands of the Thero-Brachypodietea. The stand is entirely dependent on undisturbed sand and on the seasonal rainfall that triggers germination; trampling or sand extraction removes it directly. It sits within the wider Mediterranean and Macaronesian grey dune grassland belt and is told apart from the perennial swards around it, such as those with Crucianella maritima (2210) or Euphorbia terracina (2220), by its therophyte-dominated, markedly seasonal aspect.

Meso- and thermo-Mediterranean dune grassland corresponding to the dunal expression of the pseudo-steppe grasslands with grasses and annuals of the Thero-Brachypodietea, built around Brachypodium species on oligotrophic, base-rich, often calcareous dune sand. The sward is mostly open and short, xerophile and rich in therophytes, occupying stabilised ground within the wider Mediterranean and Macaronesian grey dune grassland mosaic. Diagnostic material for the type itself is limited; distinguishing it from the other Brachypodietalia and Malcolmietalia dune grasslands rests on the dominance of perennial Brachypodium tussocks over the annual-dominated swards of 2230.

Juniper formations of Mediterranean and thermo-Atlantic coastal dune slopes and slacks, built by Juniperus turbinata subsp. turbinata, J. macrocarpa, J. navicularis or J. oxycedrus in the alliance Juniperion lyciae, and by Juniperus communis on calcareous dunes further north, including the Jutland dune juniper stands and the J. phoenicea subsp. lycia communities of the Rièges woods in the Camargue. The scrub forms a low, often dense and long-lived canopy over stabilised sand, more permanent than the surrounding grey dune grassland and less closed than wooded dunes proper. It sits within the broader Mediterranean dune scrub belt, from which it is distinguished by the dominance of Juniperus species with associates such as Phillyrea angustifolia, Smilax aspera and Lonicera implexa. Long-lived and slow to regenerate after fire, which is its principal threat.

Sclerophyllous, evergreen scrub of dunes in the Mediterranean and warm-temperate humid regions, structurally similar to inland Mediterranean garrigue but developed on dune sand rather than rocky or clay ground. Related western acidophilous garrigue on thin, acidic soils carries species such as Cistus ladanifer, Cistus calycinus, Lavandula pedunculata, Erica australis, E. umbellata and Genista hirsuta, alongside the broader Mediterranean dune scrub with Juniperus, Phillyrea and Smilax aspera. The vegetation is shaped by fire and grazing history, resprouting readily after burning and often derived from clearance of dune woodland. Little further descriptive material is available for the type specifically; in the field it is separated from the juniper-dominated scrub of 2250 by the dominance of Cistus and Lavandula rather than Juniperus, and from wooded dunes by its open, shrubby structure.

Coastal dune forest of the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions dominated by thermophilous pines, chiefly Pinus pinea and P. pinaster, with P. halepensis locally, and an understorey that can include Juniperus macrocarpa and J. turbinata subsp. turbinata. Many stands are of planted origin and represent a substitution stage for, occasionally the artificial equivalent of, evergreen oak forest of the Quercetalia ilicis or Ceratonio-Rhamnetalia. Beneath the pine canopy grow sclerophyllous and Mediterranean scrub species such as Pistacia lentiscus, Rhamnus alaternus, Phillyrea angustifolia, Smilax aspera and Rubia peregrina. Where shrubs come to exceed pine cover, the stand passes into Mediterranean dune scrub rather than forest. Distinguished from the broadleaved wooded dunes of 2180 by the coniferous, pine-dominated canopy, and threatened chiefly by fire and by conversion of planted stands.

Heath of quartzic, redeposited glacial sand on the dune plains of the North Sea and Baltic coasts, dominated by Calluna vulgaris with Genista anglica and G. pilosa. The substrate is highly siliceous and oligotrophic in the Netherlands, northern Belgium and northwestern Germany, becoming progressively less extreme and more continental in species composition through northeastern Germany, Poland and the eastern Baltic plain. The larger dune systems carry a distinctive assemblage of interacting communities and harbour many specialised, localised organisms, but the type has regressed considerably and surviving stands are fragile and often threatened by nutrient enrichment and by afforestation. Distinguished from the true coastal Empetrum dune heaths of 2140 and 2320 mainly by geographic position on the inland edge of the dune plain rather than on the active dune ridge itself, and from inland dry heath by its position on this glacial sand landscape.

Coastal, non-dunal heath on quartzic sand of glacial origin, dominated by Calluna vulgaris together with Empetrum nigrum, occurring behind the active dune belt on the North Sea and Baltic coasts. It shares its substrate and general physiognomy with the Calluna-Genista heaths of 2310, from which it is separated by the co-dominance of Empetrum nigrum rather than Genista species, and it stands apart from the genuinely dune-bound Empetrum heaths of 2140 by its non-dunal, more inland position on the reworked glacial sand plain. As with related heaths, the vegetation depends on continued low-intensity use or natural nutrient poverty to resist encroachment by scrub and woodland, and is vulnerable to nitrogen deposition and to conversion of the underlying sandy ground.

Open, often species-poor grassland of dry, siliceous inland dune sand of Atlantic, sub-Atlantic and Mediterranean-montane distribution, with a strong component of annuals. Two closely related forms occur: pioneer stands of unstable Germano-Baltic fluvioglacial sand with Corynephorus canescens, Carex arenaria, Spergula morisonii and Teesdalia nudicaulis, carpeted with fruticose lichens of the genera Cladonia and Cetraria, and grassland of more stabilised inland dune systems with Agrostis species and Corynephorus canescens or other acidophilous grasses. The vegetation depends on continued sand instability or on nutrient-poor, disturbed ground; stabilisation, nutrient enrichment or afforestation all remove it. Distinguished from coastal dune grassland types by its inland setting on relict glacial sand deposits, and from surrounding closed grassland or heath by its open, often lichen-rich sward and dominance of Corynephorus canescens.

Sparsely vegetated inland dunes of the Pannonian plain and adjacent basins, forming mosaics of open shifting sand, dune lichen carpets, pioneer swards rich in annuals, and closed dry grassland. Soils are loose, calcareous to slightly acid sands with almost no water retention and strong summer heating. Diagnostic species include the lichens Cladonia convoluta and C. furcata, together with Corynephorus canescens, Thymus serpyllum, Viola tricolor subsp. tricolor, Cerastium semidecandrum and Alyssum montanum subsp. gmelinii; in Austria the association Thymo angustifolii-Corynephoretum canescentis marks fragmentary stands at disturbed sites. The type owes its historic extent to hay harvesting and grazing, which kept the sand open; without this use it stabilises and closes into grassland or scrub within a few decades. Only the full mosaic of open sand, lichen crust and pioneer or closed swards counts here; steppes and meadow steppes on stabilised sand not tied to a dune relief belong to 6260 instead.

Nutrient-poor standing waters on whose shores two related vegetation types occur on nutrient-poor sediments: perennial amphibious swards of the Littorelletalia uniflorae along stable water-land interfaces, and short-lived pioneer vegetation of the Isoeto-Nanojuncetea on banks that dry out periodically; the two often occur together but may also stand separately. Both are built from small, low-growing ephemerophytes tolerant of fluctuating water levels. Characteristic Littorelletea species are Littorella uniflora, Potamogeton polygonifolius, Pilularia globulifera, Juncus bulbosus subsp. bulbosus and Eleocharis acicularis; the Isoeto-Nanojuncetea component is marked by Elatine species, Eleocharis ovata, Juncus tenageia, Cyperus fuscus and Limosella aquatica. The German classification records this vegetation on mesotrophic natural lakes and on self-developing gravel and clay pits; the corresponding EUNIS type covers only the exposed-shore pioneer stage and is narrower than this Annex type. Eutrophication, bank fixation and constant water levels remove the type by closing the amphibious zone.

Very shallow Mediterranean ponds, only a few centimetres deep, filled in winter and spring and dry for the rest of the year, carrying a flora of Mediterranean therophytes and geophytes rather than the amphibious perennials of comparable northern habitats. Vegetation belongs to the alliances Isoetion, Nanocyperion flavescentis, Preslion cervinae, Agrostion salmanticae, Heleochloion and Lythrion tribracteati, arranged in concentric zones that track the drying sequence. Characteristic, often endemic species include Isoetes species such as I. histrix and I. duriei, Damasonium alisma, Eryngium corniculatum, Ranunculus lateriflorus, Crypsis species and orchids of the genus Serapias. On the Azores the type is represented by the Anthemido-Menthetum pulegii association. The habitat depends entirely on the natural hydroperiod; drainage, levelling, ploughing and eutrophication from adjacent land use destroy it, usually irreversibly given the narrow endemism of much of its flora.

Open pioneer vegetation of herbaceous and sub-shrubby plants colonising the unstable gravel beds of streams with an alpine flow regime, high in summer from snowmelt and low the rest of the year, in the alpine and subalpine belts of the high mountains and in boreal and lower Arctic hills further north. Two altitudinal forms are distinguished, a higher one dominated by Epilobium fleischeri with Saxifraga species, Dryas octopetala and Gypsophila repens, and a lower, montane one with Chondrilla chondrilloides, Calamagrostis pseudophragmites and seedlings of riparian willows such as Salix elaeagnos and Myricaria germanica. The vegetation is repeatedly reset by flood and gravel movement, which keeps it permanently pioneer; regulation of the flow regime and channel fixation remove the disturbance the type depends on and let it close into scrub. It grades downstream into the willow and Myricaria scrub of 3230 as sediment stabilises.

Low pioneer shrub vegetation of Myricaria germanica and willows that invades the herbaceous gravel-bar communities of alpine-regime mountain and boreal streams once fine silt begins to accumulate in the deposits. The Salici-Myricarietum association is the characteristic form, built from Myricaria germanica together with Salix elaeagnos, S. purpurea subsp. gracilis, S. daphnoides and S. nigricans on periodically flooded shoals. As a pioneer stage it needs recurrent flooding and fresh sediment to persist; without disturbance it develops into taller willow and Salix elaeagnos scrub of 3240 and eventually into riparian forest, while flow regulation removes the flood pulses the shrubs depend on and lets the gravel bars grow over with terrestrial vegetation instead. It is distinguished from 3220 by the presence of an established woody layer, and from 3240 by the continuing dominance of Myricaria over taller Salix stands.

Taller thickets and open woods on higher, less frequently flooded gravel shoals of alpine and peri-Alpine mountain streams, built from Salix elaeagnos, S. purpurea subsp. gracilis, S. daphnoides, S. nigricans and Hippophae rhamnoides, sometimes accompanied by Alnus or Betula. It follows the lower Myricaria scrub of 3230 in the succession from bare gravel to riparian forest as sediment banks rise and stabilise further above normal flow. Hippophae rhamnoides is a useful field marker where it occurs, since it is largely restricted to this later, drier stage rather than to the actively reworked bars of 3220 and 3230. Channelisation and damming that stop the periodic reworking of gravel let the type either persist as a relict stand cut off from its dynamic, or succeed directly into closed alluvial forest, both of which remove the type as defined.

Pioneer vegetation of the Glaucion flavi colonising gravel deposits of Mediterranean rivers that carry water year round but with markedly reduced summer flow. Glaucium flavum is the name giving and most conspicuous species, growing with Erucastrum nasturtiifolium, Oenothera biennis and, where conditions allow, Myricaria germanica on the coarser bars. Because the type is confined to permanently flowing Mediterranean watercourses, it separates from the intermittently flowing rivers of 3290 by the continuity of the flow and from the finer, muddy Chenopodion and Bidention vegetation of 3270 by the coarser gravel substrate. Bank regulation, gravel extraction and the damming that eliminates the summer low-flow disturbance regime all remove the open, repeatedly reworked ground the type requires.

Annual, nitrophilous pioneer vegetation of muddy river banks in the lowlands and submontane belt, belonging to the Chenopodion rubri and Bidention alliances. The banks appear bare through spring and early summer and only develop their cover of Chenopodium rubrum, Bidens frondosa, Xanthium species and Polygonum lapathifolium later in the season as water levels drop; under unfavourable conditions the vegetation stays sparse or fails to appear at all. The German classification records the type on periodically exposed, herb-rich mud flats along running water. It occupies the fine sediment end of a substrate gradient that runs from the coarse gravel bars of 3220 and 3250 to these mud banks, and is removed wherever bank regulation eliminates the seasonal exposure of soft sediment.

Nitrophilous grass and sedge vegetation on the alluvial banks of large, permanently flowing Mediterranean rivers, dominated by Paspalum paspaloides, P. vaginatum, Polypogon viridis and Cyperus fuscus, backed by hanging curtains of Salix species and Populus alba on the higher bank. The herbaceous fringe stands at the wet, frequently inundated end of the bank profile, while the tree curtain marks the transition to gallery forest further from the water. Because the constituent communities are shared with other Mediterranean river types, the description here draws mainly on the Paspalo-Agrostidion sward itself. The type separates from the intermittent rivers of 3290 by its year-round flow and from finer, muddy pioneer vegetation further downstream by its perennial, grass-dominated cover.

The intermittent counterpart of 3280, occupying river beds of the same Paspalo-Agrostidion type but with an interrupted flow regime that leaves the channel completely dry or reduced to isolated pools for part of the year. Where standing pools persist, aquatic species such as Polygonum amphibium, Ranunculus fluitans and Potamogeton species including P. natans, P. nodosus and P. pectinatus can establish alongside the bank vegetation. The defining feature against 3280 is precisely this seasonal interruption of flow rather than any difference in the bank community itself; against the Mediterranean temporary ponds of 3170 it is distinguished by its linear, channel-bound form rather than a standing water body. Water abstraction that turns a naturally intermittent regime permanent, or a permanent river into one that dries completely, shifts stands out of this type in either direction.

Humid, peaty to semi-peaty heaths of the Atlantic and subatlantic lowlands and foothills, distinct from blanket bog, dominated by Erica tetralix on shallow, acid, nutrient-poor peat and peaty mineral soil that stays wet for much of the year and is often seasonally waterlogged. Typical settings are wet depressions and seepage zones within drier heathland, or marginal rings around bogs where drainage of the deeper peat can locally widen the type at the expense of the bog itself. Alongside Erica tetralix, Juncus squarrosus, Trichophorum cespitosum, Molinia caerulea, Calluna vulgaris, Sphagnum compactum and Gentiana pneumonanthe are diagnostic. Traditional grazing and sod cutting have long maintained the open structure; drainage or abandonment tips the type either towards drier heath or, where nutrients rise, towards Molinia grassland. The oceanic variant with Erica vagans and Schoenus nigricans on more base rich ground is included here as a regional form.

Hygrophilous heaths of the temperate oceanic climate on semi-peaty or dried peaty soils with a mineral surface layer, distinguished from 4010 by the constant presence of Erica ciliaris or, in its place, the closely related endemic Erica mackaiana. The type belongs to the alliances Genistion micrantho-anglicae and Ulicion minoris, with named associations including Ulici minoris-Ericetum ciliaris, Ulici gallii-Ericetum mackaianae and Cirsio filipenduli-Ericetum ciliaris. Alongside the diagnostic Erica species, Genista anglica, G. micrantha and Sphagnum species accompany the sward. The distribution is narrow, restricted to the western seaboard of Europe with its exceptionally oceanic winters, which makes drainage and afforestation of these heaths a loss with little prospect of recolonisation elsewhere. Where Erica ciliaris and E. mackaiana are absent, the stand belongs to the wider 4010 rather than here.

Dwarf-shrub heaths on acid, nutrient-poor, free-draining soils and podsols in the Atlantic and subatlantic lowlands and low mountains, dominated by Calluna vulgaris with Vaccinium myrtillus, V. vitis-idaea, Genista pilosa or Erica cinerea according to region. Most stands are secondary, kept open for centuries by grazing, burning, sod-cutting and litter raking on ground too poor for arable use, and they close into birch and pine woodland within decades once that use stops. Regional forms run from submontane Vaccinium-Calluna heaths of the Hercynian ranges and the lower Alps through the low Calluna-Genista heaths of the Germano-Baltic lowlands to the oceanic Erica heaths of the western seaboard. Wet heaths with Erica tetralix on peaty ground belong to 4010, alpine dwarf-shrub communities above the tree line to 4060; the boundary is drawn by soil moisture and altitude, not by the dominant shrub.

Dry coastal heaths of the temperate Atlantic seaboard on well drained soil, dominated by Erica vagans, often but not necessarily with Ulex europaeus; the type excludes prostrate maritime dwarf formations closer to the shore. It occupies free draining, nutrient poor, acid siliceous ground and is typically maintained by grazing and burning as a secondary vegetation derived from clearance of acidophilous woodland. The presence of Ulex europaeus is not required for the type to be recognised, since Erica vagans alone can carry the full diagnostic weight. It sits within the wider family of Atlantic dry heaths and is distinguished from the wet heaths of 4010 and 4020 by its dry, well aerated substrate rather than by any single species, and from the alpine and boreal heaths of 4060 by its lowland coastal position.

Ericaceous scrub of low to medium height, endemic to Macaronesia and built from different alliances on the two archipelagos: Fayo-Ericion arboreae and Telino-Adenocarpion foliolosae in the Canary Islands, Daboecion azoricae and related associations in the Azores. Erica arborea and E. platycodon dominate widely, joined on the Canaries by Chamaecytisus proliferus subsp. proliferus and Ilex canariensis, and on the Azores by Daboecia azorica, Juniperus brevifolia, Laurus azorica and Myrica faya. Diagnostic Azorean species include Lysimachia azorica, Thymus caespititius and Vaccinium cylindraceum. The vegetation colonises thin soils on pyroclastic debris, lava and rock outcrops, often cyclically renewed by volcanic or erosive disturbance, and can succeed towards laurel forest where conditions allow. Floristic composition differs markedly between and even within the archipelagos, so the type is best read island by island rather than as a single uniform community.

A broad family of low, dwarf or prostrate shrub formations of the alpine and subalpine belts of the Eurasian mountain systems and of boreal and Arctic hills further north, dominated variously by ericaceous shrubs, Dryas octopetala, dwarf junipers or greenweeds according to exposure, snow lie, substrate and region. Windswept, largely snow free ridges carry single layered Loiseleuria procumbens mats with prostrate Vaccinium species; more sheltered acid podsols in the Alps, Carpathians and Balkan ranges carry Rhododendron dominated heath, often two layered with Vaccinium myrtillus and V. vitis-idaea beneath; calcareous ground in the Alps and Dinarides instead carries Rhododendron hirsutum and Erica herbacea heath. Mountain dwarf juniper scrub and, on high southern nemoral mountains, low Genista or Chamaecytisus heaths complete the family. Field identification rests on matching the dominant shrub and its companions to the regional subtype rather than on a single combination; it separates from the ericoid heath EUNIS S22 mainly by covering the broader alpine and boreal range rather than one regional facies.

Krummholz scrub of Pinus mugo, usually with an understorey or admixture of Rhododendron species, occupying dry sites in the eastern inner Alps, the northern and southeastern outer Alps, the Carpathians, the Apennines, the Dinarides and the Balkan Range, at the transition between subalpine forest and alpine grassland. The German classification names it Alpenrosengebüsch or Latschengebüsch depending on which element dominates. Rhododendron hirsutum, R. ferrugineum and, in the eastern part of the range, R. myrtifolium accompany Pinus mugo, together with Rhodothamnus chamaecistus, Calamagrostis villosa and Homogyne alpina. The community occupies calcareous to intermediate substrates drier than those carrying pure Rhododendron heath, and forms a stable, naturally treeless facies at the upper forest limit rather than a stage in a succession; grazing pressure and clearance at the edge of its range are the main threats where the type meets managed alpine pasture.

Subarctic and boreo-alpine willow scrub of the Scottish Highlands, the Icelandic and Scandinavian mountains, and analogous stands in the Alps, Pyrenees, Cantabrian Mountains and Carpathians, often following watercourses. Regional subtypes include the alpigenous small willow brush of the Alps, Apennines, Jura and western Hercynian ranges, the Pyreneo-Cantabric willow brush, the Hercynio-Carpathian willow brush with associations such as Salicetum lapponum, and the boreo-alpine willow brush proper in Scotland, Iceland and Scandinavia. The scrub is built from small shrubby Salix species, among them S. lapponum, S. lanata, S. arbuscula, S. myrsinites and S. glauca, standing 0.5 to 2 metres tall. It differs from the taller subalpine deciduous scrub of EUNIS S25 in its more open, lower stature, and from riparian Salix scrub of lowland floodplains in its montane to subarctic, snow influenced setting rather than an alluvial one.

Cushion-forming, often spiny dwarf shrub heaths of the highest, driest mountains of the Mediterranean and Irano-Turanian regions, above or at the treeline, on shallow, mostly base-rich soils exposed to wind and frost. Primary stands occupy screes and summit ridges; secondary, zoogenic stands of the same species extend downslope where grazing has opened the ground. Composition is strongly regional: Echinospartum horridum in the Pyrenees, Erinacea anthyllis and Vella spinosa in the Sierra Nevada, Astragalus sirinicus and Genista corsica or G. salzmannii on Corsica and Sardinia, Astragalus angustifolius across the Greek mountains and Crete, and broom-like Spartocytision nubigeni scrub above 1900 metres on the Canary Islands. The dense, hemispherical cushions of Astragalus, Genista, Erinacea and related genera, close-set and often spiny, are the field character common to all forms. Related but lower-altitude hedgehog-heaths of the eastern Mediterranean supra- and oromediterranean belt are counted here only in part; garrigues and phryganas of the thermo- and mesomediterranean lowlands belong to other types.

Low deciduous scrub of continental and submediterranean character, confined to the Pannonian basin and its margins: the eastern Alpine periphery, the southern Carpathian foothills, the Transylvanian plateau and the northern Balkan hills. It grows on both calcareous and siliceous ground, usually in mosaic with steppe grassland and rupicolous Pannonic grassland, often fringing woodland. Dominants include Cerasus fruticosa and C. mahaleb, Amygdalus nana, Spiraea media and S. crenata, Rosa spinosissima and R. gallica, Amelanchier ovalis and Cotoneaster species, with an admixture of steppe herbs such as Nepeta pannonica, Aster linosyris and Vincetoxicum hirundinaria. Where scrub becomes low and clonal, dominated by Prunus fruticosa or Caragana frutex within dry grassland, it belongs to the same type; taller thorn scrub with Prunus spinosa, Crataegus monogyna and Cornus sanguinea is the widespread temperate counterpart and is distinguished mainly by its wider, non-Pannonic range.

Closed thickets dominated by Potentilla fruticosa at around 1550 metres in the west Rhodope mountains of Bulgaria, set within the belt of Picea abies and Pinus sylvestris forest. The type is narrowly localised and species-poor: besides the dominant shrub, the sward carries Bellardiochloa violacea, Galium boreale and G. verum, Geum rhodopeum, Nardus stricta and the Rhodope endemics Veronica rhodopaea and Viola rhodopeia, with the moss Abietinella abietina in the ground layer. Recognition rests on the closed cover of Potentilla fruticosa itself, a shrub rarely dominant elsewhere in European vegetation at this altitude. Superficially similar willow scrub of wet, groundwater-fed ground belongs to a different, much more widespread type and is separated by its permanently waterlogged soils, which this montane thicket does not require.

Deciduous thickets of the wooded steppe zone of the Pontic and Sarmatic regions, occurring within and around the range of the easternmost steppe oak woods with which they form a landscape complex. Several associations are endemic to Dobrogea, among them Asphodelino luteae-Paliuretum and Rhamno catharticae-Jasminietum fruticantis. Dominant shrubs are Prunus spinosa, Crataegus monogyna, Caragana frutex, Spiraea crenata and Amygdalus nana, together with Paliurus spina-christi, Jasminum fruticans and Rhamnus cathartica; the herb layer carries steppe species such as Asphodeline lutea, Paeonia tenuifolia, Dianthus nardiformis and Salvia ringens. Recognition rests on this combination of thorny pontic shrubs with steppe herbs on the dry, treeless margins of the steppe-woodland mosaic. Taller thorn scrub of the temperate lowlands with the same dominant shrubs but without the steppe herb layer belongs to the widespread submediterranean type rather than here.

Stable, calcicolous scrub of hill and montane levels dominated by Buxus sempervirens, thermophilous and drought-tolerant, growing on calcareous or, more rarely, siliceous ground. It forms the natural woodland edge of dry, box-rich calcareous forest, fringed by tall-herb communities of the Geranion sanguinei alliance with species such as Geranium sanguineum and Dictamnus albus. Accompanying shrubs are Prunus mahaleb, Cornus mas, Berberis vulgaris, Ligustrum vulgare, Viburnum lantana and Amelanchier ovalis. In the euro-siberian part of its range the more open stands carry a noticeable submediterranean flora. Unlike much thorn scrub, the type is stable rather than a stage in succession: closed Buxus stands persist for long periods on the same rocky slopes without passing into forest. Boundaries against ordinary thorn scrub and against Mediterranean pseudomaquis rest on the dominance of Buxus itself rather than on the accompanying species, which overlap with both.

Scrub of the higher levels, upper montane to subalpine and oromediterranean, of the south-western European mountains, dominated by Cytisus purgans on shallow, superficial soils. Stands often stand alongside dwarf juniper scrub or hedgehog-heaths and, physiognomically, closely resemble the latter: low, dense, wiry shrub cover with little herb layer beneath. The single diagnostic species named for the type is Cytisus purgans itself, whose broom-like, leafless green stems distinguish it in the field from both juniper scrub and true hedgehog-heaths, which are built from spiny cushion shrubs rather than brooms. Given this narrow floristic basis, the type is best recognised by physiognomy and altitude together with the dominant species, rather than by a diagnostic species combination.

Formations of Juniperus communis from the lowlands to the montane belt, arising as a successional stage rather than as a distinct plant community in its own right. Most commonly it develops on mesophilous to xerophilous, nutrient-poor calcareous grassland of the Festuco-Brometea, grazed or left fallow, and more rarely on Calluna heathland; the juniper cover ranges from scattered, ancient bushes to dense stands that shade out the underlying grassland. Accompanying species reflect the grassland or heath it derives from: on calcareous ground the typical Festuco-Brometea flora, on heaths Calluna vulgaris, Vaccinium myrtillus, Empetrum nigrum and Nardus stricta. Recognition in the field rests on Juniperus communis growing over, and clearly succeeding, one of these two vegetation types rather than on an independent species combination. As grazing intensifies or stops entirely, the juniper cover either fails to establish or closes into scrub that eventually gives way to woodland.

Low scrub and garrigue of dolomitic tableland, karst, sand and terra rossa in the far south-west of Portugal, exceptionally rich in narrow endemics. Two named associations characterise it, Ulicetum erinacei and Genisto triacanthi-Cistetum palhinhae, the latter built around the endemic Cistus palhinhae. Accompanying species include Genista hirsuta subsp. algarbiensis, G. triacanthos, Juniperus turbinata, Ulex erinaceus, Sideritis arborescens subsp. lusitanica and the strict local endemics Biscutela vicentina and Serratula monardii var. algarbiensis. Recognition rests on this combination of local endemics, above all Cistus palhinhae and Ulex erinaceus, restricted to the Algarve and neighbouring Alentejo coast; the type is not defined by a wetland character despite the traditional name, and separation from ordinary Mediterranean garrigue on comparable substrates rests entirely on the presence of these endemics.

Mediterranean and submediterranean evergreen sclerophyllous scrub organised around tree-form, arborescent junipers rather than the low shrubs typical of most matorral. Dominance shifts regionally between species: Juniperus oxycedrus and J. phoenicea in the western and central Mediterranean, J. excelsa and J. foetidissima in Greece, Anatolia and the Near East, J. communis in scattered Mediterranean stands, J. drupacea restricted to the Peloponnese and Asia Minor, and J. thurifera in continental mountain areas; mixed stands of two or more species also occur. Recognition in the field is straightforward once the arborescent, tree-like growth form of the junipers is distinguished from the low, hemispherical shrubs of hedgehog-heath and phrygana. As a stage in scrub succession it can grade into open juniper woodland on one side and into lower, denser maquis on the other, from which it is separated chiefly by the emergent stature of the junipers.

Pre-desert deciduous scrub of the arid south-western Iberian peninsula, confined to the thermo-Mediterranean xerophytic climate of the Almeria region. It represents the mature, climax phase of the local vegetation series and is built around tall stands of Zyziphus lotus, accompanied by Periploca laevigata, Lycium intricatum, Asparagus stipularis and A. albus and Withania frutescens. Named associations include Ziziphetum loti, Zizipho-Maytenetum europaei and Mayteno-Periplocetum. Recognition rests on the emergent, hummock-forming Zyziphus lotus itself, which gives the scrub a distinctive rounded, thorny structure unlike any other European vegetation. Confined to a narrow arid corner of Europe, the type is threatened wherever the low, extensive land use of its native area gives way to irrigation or urbanisation.

Humid arborescent matorral built around tall Laurus nobilis, occurring in oceanic, sheltered stations of the Iberian peninsula. In Spain it appears as a facies of Viburno tini-Fraxinetum orni rich in Laurus nobilis in the southern mountains of Valencia, and as a laurel-rich facies of Lauro-Quercetum ilicis from Asturias to the Basque Country. Accompanying species include Arbutus unedo, Ceratonia siliqua, Fraxinus ornus, Phillyrea latifolia, Quercus ilex, Olea europaea var. sylvestris and Viburnum tinus, together with lianas such as Smilax aspera and Rubia peregrina. Recognition rests on Laurus nobilis reaching tree stature and forming a closed or near-closed canopy, rather than occurring as scattered individuals; small relic laurophyllous forests of the Atlantic coast with a similar canopy but a different, more oceanic associated flora are treated separately. Where the same species combination forms lower, denser thicket rather than tall matorral, it is assigned to the related type of Laurus nobilis thickets.

Lower, shrubbier facies of the arborescent Laurus nobilis matorral, generally confined to humid or cool stations. The material available names only the single dominant species, Laurus nobilis; no separate associated flora or syntaxa are recorded for this facies beyond what applies to the taller matorral it derives from. Recognition in the field therefore rests on Laurus nobilis dominating a stand of thicket rather than tree height, on sites moister or cooler than typical Mediterranean scrub. Distinguishing it from the arborescent matorral with Laurus nobilis is a matter of stature alone: where the laurel reaches closed tree canopy the taller type applies, where it stays at shrub height on the same kind of humid ground this lower facies applies.

Low, cushion-like formations dominated by Helichrysum italicum, in immediate contact with sea cliffs, forming the transition between true cliff vegetation or clifftop phrygana and thermo-Mediterranean scrub further inland. Spurges, chiefly Euphorbia pithyusa, grow through the Helichrysum together with Pistacia lentiscus, Camphorosma monspeliaca, Artemisia densiflora and species of Thymelaea such as T. hirsuta and T. tartonraira. Recognition rests on this narrow coastal position, immediately behind the cliff-edge vegetation proper, and on the combination of Helichrysum italicum with spurge and Thymelaea species rather than on any single dominant. Because it sits between two other, better-defined vegetation belts, it is best identified by its intermediate position in the field as much as by its species list.

A broad group of thermo-Mediterranean scrub formations, largely indifferent to whether the substrate is calcareous or siliceous, together with a set of strongly distinctive, thermophile formations endemic to southern Iberia. Named sub-formations include Genista fasselata brush of the eastern Mediterranean, Crataegus azarolus scrub of Cyprus, tree-spurge stands of Euphorbia dendroides on Mediterranean islands, diss-garrigue dominated by tall tussocks of Ampelodesmos mauritanicus on the Tyrrhenian coast and in Sicily, palmetto brush built around Chamaerops humilis in south-western and southern Iberia, Mediterranean pre-desert scrub of the arid south-east Spanish provinces, thermo-Mediterranean broom fields of Lygos, Cytisus and Genista species, and spiny spurge garrigue of Euphorbia melitensis on Malta. Given this diversity, recognition proceeds sub-formation by sub-formation, through the named dominant, rather than through a single shared species combination; several of the south-eastern Spanish stands survive only in a few undisturbed localities and are gravely at risk.

Rare, extremely local cushion-forming associations of thermo-Mediterranean clifftops and their immediate surroundings, scattered along the western Mediterranean coast. The type is carried by Astragalus massiliensis or, in other stands, by Anthyllis hermanniae, both variously accompanied by Thymelaea hirsuta, Helichrysum italicum, Plantago subulatum and Armeria ruscinonensis. Recognition rests on this small set of cushion-forming species occupying an isolated clifftop position, with no single association covering more than a few sites. Because stands are so few and so local, each occurrence carries disproportionate conservation weight; superficially similar cushion vegetation of other Mediterranean coasts, built from different dominants, belongs to separate types.

Low, thorny formations of hemispherical shrubs occupying the coastal thermo-Mediterranean zone of the eastern Mediterranean: the Aegean islands, mainland Greece, the Ionian islands and coastal Anatolia, where they are considerably more widespread and floristically richer than comparable western Mediterranean phrygana. The type is carried by Sarcopoterium spinosum together with Centaurea spinosa, Satureja thymbra, Thymus capitatus, Genista acanthoclada, Anthyllis hermanniae, Cistus creticus and Pistacia lentiscus, among a long list of accompanying chamaephytes. Recognition in the field rests on the dense, low, spiny hemispherical growth form of Sarcopoterium spinosum itself, sharply different from the taller, softer thorn scrub of temperate Europe. A few rare, relict associations of similar appearance occur on western Mediterranean seashores and cliffs, forming a narrow belt between cliff communities and thermo-Mediterranean brush.

A set of cushion-forming, often thorny, summer-deciduous sclerophyllous formations, each endemic to a small Mediterranean island area and treated together for their shared physiognomy rather than a shared flora. Sub-types include mid-elevation phrygana of Crete with Euphorbia acanthothamnos, Verbascum spinosum and Sideritis syriaca at the contact between phrygana and hedgehog-heath, isolated Hypericum aegyptiacum colonies on coastal rocks of the Ionian islands, western Crete, Sardinia and Lampedusa, impoverished Sarcopoterium spinosum stands of southern Sardinia and the Gulf of Taranto, Genista acanthoclada phrygana of north-western Sardinia, Balearic clifftop phrygana with the endemics Launaea cervicornis, Astragalus balearicus and Centaurea balearica, Cyrno-Sardian Genista corsica or G. morisii phrygana of Corsican and Sardinian headlands, and Pantelleria phrygana with the local endemics Helichrysum saxatile subsp. errerae and Matthiola pulchella. Given this island-by-island endemism, each sub-type is recognised by its own local dominant rather than by a shared diagnostic combination.

Open, sparse pioneer vegetation on very shallow, superficial calcareous or otherwise base-rich soils, in places on basic volcanic substrate, dominated by annuals and succulents of the Alysso alyssoidis-Sedion albi. A priority habitat. Cover is patchy, built from small rosette plants and succulents with a rich cryptogam component, on rock ledges, thin rendzinas and similar skeletal ground from the lowlands into the mountains, wherever soil stays too thin and dry for a closed sward. Recognisable by Sedum album, S. acre, Alyssum alyssoides, Saxifraga tridactylites, Hornungia petraea and Teucrium botrys, with Jovibarba and Sempervivum species on the rockiest ground and mosses such as Abietinella abietina and Homalothecium sericeum filling the gaps. The type persists only as long as shallow soil keeps the site open; deeper soil lets denser calcareous grassland take over. Similar swards on artificial substrates such as walls and quarry spoil are excluded.

Dry, mostly open grasslands on more or less calcareous sand, with a subcontinental centre of distribution on inland dune systems, river terraces and sandy plains of the lowlands. Stands are short and patchy, dominated by narrow-leaved grasses such as Koeleria glauca and Festuca psammophila over a low, drought-tolerant herb layer. Recognisable by Alyssum montanum ssp. gmelinii, Astragalus arenarius, Carex ligerica, C. praecox, Dianthus deltoides, Euphorbia seguieriana, Gypsophila fastigiata, Helichrysum arenarium, Herniaria glabra, Petrorhagia prolifera and Silene chlorantha, with Sedum reflexum and Allium schoenoprasum on the driest ridges. The nutrient-poor, base-rich sand and the summer drought keep the sward permanently open, so closure by scrub is slow. The related EUNIS sand grassland of the same region is distinguished by its acid to neutral, not calcareous, sandy soils, which carry a largely different, more acidophilous flora even where the two occur close together on the same dune system.

Generally open grassland of specialised, heavy-metal-tolerant plants, on three kinds of ground: natural rock outcrops enriched in zinc or lead, river gravels and shingles carrying such metals, and old spoil heaps and terrils around historic mines. The flora consists of metallophyte races otherwise rare or absent from ordinary soils: Viola calaminaria, heavy-metal races of Noccaea (Thlaspi) caerulescens, Armeria maritima, Minuartia verna and Silene vulgaris, with Festuca ophioliticola in some regions, plus Campanula rotundifolia and a distinctive lichen and moss layer including Cladonia and Weissia species. The type is bound to the metal contamination itself, whether geological or mining-derived, and to the sparse, open cover that alone tolerates it. Younger, still-colonising spoil-heap vegetation lacks the threatened endemic taxa of the older stands and is not treated as priority, which is the practical line separating the two in the field.

Closed, mesophile subalpine and lower alpine grassland dominated by the tussock grass Festuca eskia, confined to the Pyrenees, where it occupies north-facing slopes and shaded depressions. Companion species include Arnica montana, Ranunculus pyrenaeus, Selinum pyrenaeum, Trifolium alpinum, Campanula barbata, Gentiana punctata and Leucorchis albida. The tight, tussocky sward and the strict restriction to shaded aspect distinguish it in the field from the surrounding, more general acidophilous alpine grassland of the wider European mountain ranges, of which it forms only the Pyrenean, Festuca eskia dominated expression.

Boreo-alpine grassland and dwarf-sedge vegetation of the highest summits, with its main range in the Alps and the Scandinavian mountains and outliers in the Carpathians, dominated by Juncus trifidus and Carex bigelowii over a substantial cover of mosses and lichens; associated snowbed communities, with Cassiope tetragona in the north, are included in the same type. Stands sit on thin, exposed, wind-scoured ground above the closed alpine turf, where snow cover is short-lived or absent and frost action dominates. The type spans both the wind-exposed ridge vegetation and the late-snow depressions in one unit, which sets it apart from the geographically narrower boreal grasslands of Fennoscandia and Scotland and from the temperate alpine grasslands of the central and southern European ranges, both of which occupy comparable positions further south or west.

Thermophile, open grassland of siliceous upper slopes and summits in the high mountains of Iberia, dominated by Festuca indigesta, with local extensions into the Euro-Siberian domain at the subalpine level. Soils are base-poor and shallow over siliceous bedrock, the growing season short and winters harsh, with strong winds keeping ridges free of snow and exposing the ground to repeated freeze-thaw. Cover is moderately open to closed, formed of prostrate or dwarf grasses and forbs with a marked endemic component: Luzula caespitosa, Jasione crispa aggr., Pilosella vahlii, Sedum brevifolium, Teesdalia conferta, Dianthus langeanus, Scorzoneroides cantabrica and Silene ciliata alongside the dominant fescue. At somewhat lower altitude in western Iberia a related, grazed grassland on similarly shallow siliceous and ultramafic soils takes over, distinguished from this type mainly by its lower elevation and its pastoral rather than purely climatic character.

Alpine and subalpine grassland of base-rich soils across the high mountain ranges of Europe, from the Alps, Pyrenees and Carpathians to the Balkan mountains, with outlying, more thermophile expressions on Corsica and in the central and southern Apennines. Dominant and characteristic plants include Dryas octopetala, Carex sempervirens and Sesleria caerulea, together with Gentiana nivalis, G. clusii, Anthyllis vulneraria, Astragalus alpinus, Draba aizoides and Phyteuma orbiculare. On the deeper soils of the lower alpine and subalpine belt closed, often grazed or mown swards prevail, while on wind-exposed ridges a sculptured, wind-clipped turf develops, and on the shallowest, most xerothermic ground open, stepped grassland forms. Associated snowbed vegetation and dwarf Salix scrub belong to the same mosaic. Heavy-metal grassland on contaminated ground, though floristically related, is treated separately; the type otherwise grades into arctic-alpine calcareous grassland further north and into Balkan and Apennine expressions further south-east.

Secondary, ungrazed grassland of the highest levels in the Azores, mixing grasses, herbs and mat-forming plants with a strong endemic component, typical of exposed or unstable rocky slopes, ledges and landslips on nutrient-poor acid soil. Species composition shifts with altitude, climate, rock type and terrain stability. Characteristic plants include Holcus rigidus, Festuca jubata, Deschampsia foliosa, Agrostis congestiflora, Luzula elegans and Festuca petraea, alongside ferns such as Diplazium caudatum and Woodwardia radicans and endemic herbs including Ranunculus cortusifolius, Rumex azorica, Sanicula azorica and Bellis azorica. As a secondary grassland it depends on the instability of its rocky sites for its continued openness, without the regular grazing that maintains comparable grassland elsewhere.

Open, pioneer rock sward on steep, dry, sun-exposed slopes of medium-altitude mountains in the Pannonian basin and adjacent regions, roughly between 150 and 900 m, over limestone, dolomite or calcareous volcanic rock such as basalt or andesite, on shallow rendzinas. Three regional expressions are distinguished: a montane to submontane, cooler-microclimate form on the calci-orophile Diantho-Seslerion swards, a species-rich, south-facing form on rendzinas around the western and southern edge of the Carpathian arc, and, on siliceous rock ledges further west, an acidocline expression. Recognisable by Festuca pallens, Bromus pannonicus, Stipa eriocaulis, S. joannis, Carex humilis, Chrysopogon gryllus, Iris pumila, Pulsatilla grandis and Anacamptis pyramidalis, with rarer endemics such as Linum dolomiticum, Vincetoxicum pannonicum and Dianthus regis-stephani in the most calcareous stands. The much broader EUNIS rocky grassland of Central and South-Eastern Europe shares the general physiognomy but extends well beyond the Pannonian range and its rendzina soils.

Dry to semi-dry calcareous grasslands of the Festuco-Brometea on shallow, base-rich soils over limestone, dolomite or marl, mostly on sun-exposed slopes and crests from the lowlands to the submontane belt. Two wings are distinguished: the steppic, subcontinental swards of the Festucetalia valesiacae and the oceanic to submediterranean ones of the Brometalia erecti. Within the latter, the primary Xerobromion swards of the shallowest ground stand beside the secondary Mesobromion swards with Bromus erectus, which arose from centuries of extensive grazing and carry the orchid richness on which the priority form rests. Stands are open to closed, built from tussock grasses and rosette herbs with Sanguisorba minor, Helianthemum nummularium, Scabiosa columbaria and Hippocrepis comosa. Once grazing or mowing stops, a fringe stage of the Trifolio-Geranietea appears first, then thermophilous scrub; fertilisation, reseeding and afforestation remove the type just as surely.

Priority pseudo-steppe of the meso- and thermo-Mediterranean zone, a mosaic of short, xerophile grassland rich in annuals on oligotrophic, often calcareous, base-rich soil. A perennial component of the Thero-Brachypodietea, dominated by Brachypodium retusum and related tussock grasses, stands alongside a purely annual component of spring-flowering therophytes typical of the Tuberarietea guttatae, with Brachypodium distachyum among its most frequent species; on gypsum or dolomite the annual swards shift towards specialised gypsophile or silico-basiphile variants. In France a further distinction runs between open, low-nitrogen pioneer swards and more closed, nitrogen-tolerant grassland of deeper soil. Grazing and trampling maintain the type by keeping the perennial tussocks open enough for the annual flora to persist; without disturbance the perennial component thickens and excludes the therophytes, while abandonment of grazing generally lets scrub advance.

Priority, species-rich Nardus grassland on siliceous soils, closed and dry to mesophile, ranging through the Atlantic, subatlantic and boreal lowlands, hills and mountains of Europe; only stands with a genuinely high species number count as this type, ground irreversibly impoverished by overgrazing is excluded. Nardus stricta itself is often subordinate to the diversity it shelters: Antennaria dioica, Arnica montana, Campanula barbata, Gentiana pneumonanthe, Hypochoeris maculata, Leucorchis albida, Meum athamanticum, Platanthera bifolia and Potentilla aurea, together with Galium saxatile and Potentilla erecta as constant companions; the grasshopper Miramella alpina is a typical faunal element. Traditional mowing or grazing, at both the lowland to submontane and the montane to high-montane level, sustains the diversity; where it stops the sward coarsens and species drop out well before scrub establishes. Distinguished from surrounding alpine grassland mainly by the dominance of Nardus and its lower, non-summit position.

Priority steppic grassland of the sub-Pannonian region, dominated by tussock grasses, chamaephytes and perennials of the Festucion vallesiacae and related alliances, xerotherme communities of south-facing slopes on rocky AC-soils or on clay-sandy sediment layers enriched with gravel, partly natural and partly of anthropogenic origin. Recognisable by Festuca vallesiaca, Stipa capillata, S. joannis, Bothriochloa ischaemum, Chrysopogon gryllus, Carex humilis and Festuca rupicola in the graminoid layer, with Iris pumila, Ranunculus illyricus, Teucrium chamaedrys, Globularia cordifolia, Astragalus onobrychis, A. excapus and Daphne cneorum among the characteristic forbs. Stands with a mainly natural origin occupy the shallowest, rockiest ground, while the anthropogenic stands on deeper, gravelly sediment reflect long grazing history; both grade into related continental steppe and meadow-steppe grassland of the wider region without a sharp physiognomic break.

Priority steppic grassland rich in perennial grasses and herbs on loess deposits of the Pannonian region, once covering large areas but today restricted to particular landforms such as loess ridges shaped by fluviatile erosion and deposition. Characteristic species include Astragalus vesicarius, A. austriacus, A. onobrychis, Crambe tataria, Nonea pulla, Salvia nemorosa, Ornithogalum pannonicum, Phlomis tuberosa, Festuca rupicola, Falcaria vulgaris, Peucedanum alsaticum and Achillea pannonica, together with Elymus hispidus and Bromus inermis in the grass layer. The sharp contraction from a once extensive loess steppe to a few surviving ridge remnants reflects long conversion of loess ground to arable land; the surviving stands are correspondingly small and fragmented, and their loess substrate, rather than any single diagnostic species, is what sets them apart from the related steppic and sandy steppe grasslands of the surrounding Pannonian basin.

Pannonic sand steppe formed by medium to tall, perennial tuft-forming grasses and suffrutescents with a distinctly patchy ground cover, together with associated communities of spring annuals, on mobile or fixed sand such as alluvial deposits and subfossil dune systems of the Pannonian basin, with similar stands in the West Pontic basin. Recognisable by Festuca vaginata, F. beckeri, Koeleria glauca, Helichrysum arenarium, Gypsophila paniculata, Bassia laniflora and Jurinea cyanoides among the plants, and by a distinctive insect fauna including the steppe bushcricket Gampsocleis glabra, the moth Callimorpha quadripunctaria and several Zygaena species.
