The climate is strongly continental, with cold winters and hot, droughty summers that keep the sand mobile and the cover open; traditional extensive sheep grazing once maintained the type over a much wider area than it now occupies, most such grazing having since been abandoned.

Priority, species-rich dry to mesic grassland of the Fennoscandian lowlands, mainly on siliceous substrates, shaped by long-term continuous grazing or mowing without fertilisation; both traditionally managed and recently abandoned stands belong to the type. Species composition varies with region, soil, moisture and management regime, but the sward is typically rich in Agrostis capillaris, Anthoxanthum odoratum, Festuca ovina, F. rubra, Galium verum, Antennaria dioica, Dianthus deltoides, Gentianella campestris, Gymnadenia conopsea, Lychnis viscaria and Primula veris; several threatened grassland fungi, including Hygrocybe, Geoglossum and Entoloma species, are also characteristic. The absence of fertilisation and the long, uninterrupted management history are what distinguish the type from ordinary improved pasture and hay meadow; once grazing or mowing stops, the fungal flora and the rarer herbs are usually the first to disappear.

Priority alvar and flat calcareous rock vegetation of the Nordic region, an exceptionally species-rich system shaped by winter cold: the thin soil layer freezes and lies under snow for much of the year, and repeated freeze-thaw action creates small patches of bare ground colonised by annual pioneers, some of them rare. On flat, weathered rock with only a shallow soil cover, freeze-thaw also builds soil polygons with a characteristic patterned vegetation, and shallow depressions, locally called vätar on Öland and Gotland, fill with water in winter and dry out, wholly or partly, in summer. On Öland a distinct subtype is dominated by Helianthemum oelandicum over a 5 to 30 cm layer of crumbling soil on almost level, extremely slowly draining ground. Recognisable by Sedum acre, S. album, Saxifraga tridactylites, Hornungia petraea, Linum catharticum and Gentianella amarella, with regional endemics such as Artemisia oelandica on Öland and Arenaria gothica on Gotland, and a rich lichen and bryophyte layer including Cetraria nivalis and Tortella tortuosa.

Xeric grassland of the eastern sub-Mediterranean zone around Trieste, Istria and the Balkan peninsula, coexisting with the steppic grassland of the Festucetalia valesiacae (6210) but developing under less continental conditions and carrying a stronger Mediterranean element. Named associations include Carici humilis-Centaureetum rupestris, Chrysopogono-Centaureetum cristatae and Danthonio-Scorzoneretum villosae. Recognisable by Carex humilis, Bromus erectus, Centaurea rupestris, Sesleria juncifolia, Trinia glauca and Festuca rupicola, with regional specialities such as Genista holopetala, Iris cengialti, Gentiana lutea and Arctostaphylos uva-ursi. Stands occupy sharply draining, base-rich soils on valley sides, dolines and sink-holes around the Adriatic seaboard and depend on extensive grazing; where grazing has declined, the type now survives mainly as patches within a mosaic of scrub and forest. The lesser continentality and the greater Mediterranean floristic element are what separate it from the closely related, more continental steppic grassland of the Festucetalia valesiacae.

Sparse, low perennial herb vegetation confined to the ultramafic outcrops of Cyprus, notably the Troodos massif and the Akamas peninsula, where serpentine, dunite, wehrlite and harzburgite weather into thin, metal rich, base rich soils. Stands form small patches of open plant cover on rocky ground and stony slopes rather than continuous swards. Two altitudinal forms are distinguished: a high altitude form above roughly 1700 m with Acinos troodi, Alyssum troodi, Anthemis plutonia and Ranunculus cadmicus var. cypricus, and a lower form around 350 to 450 m on Akamas with Alyssum akamasicum, Centaurea cyprensis and Hyacinthella millingeni. Both harbour a specialised flora with numerous Cyprus endemics tolerant of the high magnesium and heavy metal content and the low calcium supply typical of ultramafic substrates. The type is restricted to Cyprus and has no counterpart elsewhere in the Mediterranean; separation from ordinary Mediterranean base rich scree and rock vegetation rests on the ultramafic substrate and the endemic rich composition, not on physiognomy alone.

Grass steppes of the plains, plateaus and hills of the western Black Sea region, from the lower Danube basin and Transylvania across the Podolian and Central Russian plateaus to the Volga region, Orenburg and Bashkiria. The vegetation is dominated by feather grasses such as Stipa capillata, S. lessingiana and S. pulcherrima together with Festuca valesiaca, Koeleria macrantha and Dichanthium ischaemum, forming dense tussock swards on chernozem type soils under a strongly continental climate. Characteristic companions include Vinca herbacea, Salvia nutans and Iris pumila, and on the driest, stoniest sites Kochia prostrata and Artemisia species. The type covers several alliances, from Festucion valesiacae and Stipion lessingianae of the true steppe to the more local Agropyro-Kochion of saline and stony variants and the Pimpinello-Thymion zygoidi of rocky steppe on the Balkan margin. Nearly all stands are relicts of a once vast steppe belt reduced by ploughing; moderate grazing maintains the sward, abandonment favours tall grasses and scrub.

Alpine and subalpine grasslands of the central Balkan high mountains, including the Balkan Range, Rila, Pirin, the Rhodopes and Osogovo, developed at 1600 to 2900 m over crystalline rocks and other lime deficient or decalcified substrates. The sward is dominated by fescues and related grasses, chiefly Festuca paniculata, F. airoides and F. nigrescens, Bellardiochloa violacea and Calamagrostis arundinacea, with a marked share of Balkan endemics such as Festuca balcanica, F. riloensis, F. valida, Sesleria comosa and Carex bulgarica. Regionally distinct sub types are recognised, from Festuca paniculata and F. valida swards to Sesleria comosa and Agrostis rupestris grasslands, reflecting the mosaic of exposure, snow cover duration and soil depth of these summit landscapes. Notable companions include Gentiana lutea, G. punctata and Primula deorum. As acidophilous alpine grassland of siliceous high mountains it corresponds to the wider circle of temperate alpine Nardus and Festuca communities, set apart by its Balkan endemics and its southerly, sub-Mediterranean climate.

Open, park like landscape of the Iberian Peninsula in which crops, pasture or Meso-Mediterranean arborescent matorral alternate in space or in rotation beneath a fairly closed to very open canopy of native evergreen oaks, chiefly Quercus suber, Q. ilex, Q. rotundifolia and Q. coccifera. The oaks are managed by traditional pollarding and cork harvesting, and grazing by livestock keeps the ground layer open; without this combined use the type closes into denser sclerophyllous woodland or scrub. It is an important habitat for large raptors, including the Iberian imperial eagle, for cranes on passage, and for the Iberian lynx. Separation from closed evergreen oak forest rests on the open, wooded pasture structure and the continuing agricultural or pastoral use; separation from pure matorral rests on the presence of the tree canopy.

Molinia dominated meadows of the lowland to montane belts on wet, nutrient poor soils, low in nitrogen and phosphorus, that dry out in summer while remaining waterlogged for much of the growing season. Two forms are distinguished by base status: on neutral to calcareous soils with a fluctuating water table the Eu-Molinion carries Molinia caerulea with Dianthus superbus, Selinum carvifolia, Cirsium tuberosum and Serratula tinctoria; on more acid, often peaty ground the Junco-Molinion of the Molinion caeruleae alliance adds Viola persiciflora, Cirsium dissectum, Crepis paludosa and Potentilla erecta. Diagnostic species across both forms include Succisa pratensis, Carex panicea and Sanguisorba officinalis. The type depends on extensive management with a single late season cut; without it, tall herbs and scrub take over within a few years, while the type also arises as a stage in draining raised bogs. Separation from wet eutrophic hay meadows rests on the low nutrient status, from fens on the seasonal drying out of the topsoil.

Tall humid grasslands of the Mediterranean basin, extending along the Black Sea coasts, dominated by robust grasses and rushes, chiefly Scirpus holoschoenus, Molinia caerulea and Schoenus nigricans, often on damp ground within dune systems or beside seasonal watercourses. Accompanying species include Juncus maritimus and J. acutus on more saline ground, Cyperus longus, Eupatorium cannabinum and Inula viscosa on fresher soils, and orchids such as Orchis laxiflora and Dactylorhiza elata where the water table stays high into summer. The vegetation belongs to the Molinio-Holoschoenion and occupies depressions that stay moist through a dry Mediterranean summer, contrasting with the surrounding dry grassland and scrub. It grades into dune slack vegetation on sandy coasts and into inland tall humid grassland further from the sea; distinguishing the two rests on the coastal, often calcareous and locally saline setting of the Molinio-Holoschoenion proper.

Tall, nitrophilous herb communities forming narrow fringes along watercourses and at woodland edges, in two altitudinal forms. In the plains and colline belt, the Glechometalia hederaceae and Convolvuletalia sepium orders give lush stands of Filipendula ulmaria, Urtica dioica, Epilobium hirsutum, Angelica archangelica, Petasites hybridus and Aegopodium podagraria on moist, nutrient rich soils along rivers and forest margins. In the montane to alpine belt, the Betulo-Adenostyletea class produces tall herb stands with Aconitum species, Geranium sylvaticum, Trollius europaeus, Adenostyles alliariae and Cicerbita alpina, typically sheltered along streams, under scrub or on ledges. Both forms are naturally dynamic fringe vegetation rather than closed communities and often expand where grazing or mowing of adjacent grassland has stopped. Separation from riparian forest rests on the absence of a closed tree canopy, from ordinary tall herb ruderal vegetation on the water linked, semi natural setting.

Alluvial meadows of continental to subcontinental river valleys, flooded under a natural regime and belonging to the Cnidion dubii alliance. Characteristic species include Cnidium dubium, Viola persicifolia, Scutellaria hastifolia, Allium angulosum and Juncus atratus, growing on periodically inundated soils of large river floodplains. The type depends on the natural flood pulse of the river and on continued extensive use as hay meadow or pasture; river regulation, drainage and the switch to intensive grassland management remove it. It is distinguished from other wet alluvial grasslands by its Cnidion dubii species combination and its restriction to continental climate conditions, setting it apart from the more oceanic wet meadow types of Atlantic river valleys.

Alluvial meadows along large boreal rivers with placid, slow flowing reaches that freeze over every winter and flood in spring with the snowmelt. Characteristic species include Carex acuta, C. aquatilis and C. canescens, Deschampsia cespitosa, Elymus fibrosus and Phalaris arundinacea, together with Trollius europaeus and Galium boreale on somewhat drier ground. The type includes only stands not yet overgrown by trees and shrubs; traditional management as hay meadow has largely ceased, and without grazing or mowing the sward is progressively invaded by Salix triandra and other shrubs. Separation from other wet meadow and tall sedge types rests on the boreal river setting with its annual freeze thaw and spring flood regime, rather than on a distinctive species set of its own.

Tall, about one metre high meadows dominated by Calamagrostis epigejos, developed at around 1650 m in seasonally inundated depressions on serpentinised, base rich substrate in the Troodos mountains of Cyprus. The ground floods from October or November until June or July and stays wet and muddy even in summer, supporting a dense, continuous mat of Calamagrostis epigejos and Juncus littoralis. Poa pratensis, Polypogon semiverticillatus and Ornithogalum chionopilum accompany the dominants, alongside island endemics restricted to these high altitude damp places, such as Alyssum cypricum and the endangered Crocus cyprius. The type is confined to Cyprus and has no equivalent elsewhere; its combination of a serpentine substrate with a long seasonal inundation sets it apart from ordinary Mediterranean tall humid grassland, which typically occurs on non ultramafic ground at lower altitudes.

Species-rich hay meadows of the lowlands and colline belt on deep, moderately fertile soils, cut once or twice a year and never before the grasses have flowered. The sward is tall and layered, with Arrhenatherum elatius or Alopecurus pratensis over a rich mixture of herbs including Sanguisorba officinalis, Leucanthemum ircutianum, Knautia arvensis, Galium mollugo and Tragopogon pratensis. Stands belong to the Arrhenatherion and, on more acid soils in the west, to the Brachypodio-Centaureion nemoralis. Heavy fertilisation, early or frequent cutting and a shift to silage all remove the herb layer and with it the type; where cutting stops, tall herbs and scrub take over within a few years. Separation from moist hay meadows of floodplains rests on the absence of flood indicators, from montane hay meadows on the absence of Geranium sylvaticum and Trollius europaeus.

Species rich, mesophilous hay meadows of the montane to subalpine belt, mostly above 600 m, dominated by Trisetum flavescens on deep, well drained soils under a short, cool growing season. The sward carries a dense mixture of tall herbs, including Heracleum sphondylium, Astrantia major, Crepis mollis, Geranium sylvaticum, Trollius europaeus, Silene dioica, Campanula glomerata and Primula elatior, with regional additions such as Narcissus poeticus or Phyteuma orbiculare. Traditional management combines a single late cut with moderate manuring and, in many regions, aftermath grazing; the type depends on this regime and on the absence of early or frequent cutting. Abandonment leads to tall herb and scrub encroachment, while intensification through heavy fertilising or a shift to silage removes the characteristic herb layer. Separation from lowland hay meadows rests on the montane species set with Trollius europaeus and Geranium sylvaticum, absent from the Arrhenatherion of lower altitudes.

Vegetation complex of Fennoscandia combining small copses of deciduous trees and shrubs with patches of open meadow, traditionally kept open by a combination of raking, hay cutting, grazing and the pollarding or lopping of trees. Common tree species are ash, birch, pedunculate oak, small leaved lime, wych elm and grey alder, often old and pollarded, carrying a rich epiphytic flora of mosses and lichens on their bark. The herb layer is species rich, including Briza media, Primula veris, Listera ovata, Orchis mascula and Cypripedium calceolus, and supports many threatened species tied to old pollards in semi open conditions. The type includes both actively managed stands and overgrown ones that retain old pollarded or lopped trees, but not abandoned meadows now being invaded by young trees, which fall outside the type once tree cover closes. Very few stands are still under traditional management today, most surviving as small relict patches.

Humid grasslands of the alliance Molinio-Hordeion secalini, occurring along karstic rivers and in karst poljes of the Dinaric Alps, flooded or very wet in winter and spring and drying progressively through summer. The strong seasonal contrast in soil moisture brings hygrophilous species and drier grassland species together in the same stand, with Deschampsia media, Hordeum secalinum, Ranunculus sardous and Trifolium fragiferum alongside Chrysopogon gryllus and Bromus erectus. The type carries several Dinaric endemics, including Edraianthus dalmaticus, Succisella petteri and Chouardia litardierei. Traditionally used as extensive hay meadow and pasture, it occupies a naturally dry Mediterranean landscape as a locally wet exception tied to the karstic hydrology of the poljes. Separation from ordinary Mediterranean dry grassland rests on this seasonal wetness, from other wet meadow types on the Dinaric, karst linked setting and the specific species combination.

Acid, ombrotrophic bogs fed solely by rainwater, with a water table generally above that of the surrounding land and a domed peat body sustained by ongoing peat formation. The surface is a mosaic of colourful Sphagnum hummocks, lawns and pools, with Sphagnum magellanicum, S. fuscum and, in the boreal region, S. angustifolium, alongside Andromeda polifolia, Eriophorum vaginatum and Vaccinium oxycoccos on the hummocks and Carex limosa, Rhynchospora alba and Scheuchzeria palustris in the wetter lawns and pools. Active means that a significant part of the surface is still peat forming; a temporary halt after fire or drought does not exclude a bog from the type. The bog fauna includes specialist dragonflies such as Leucorrhinia dubia and Somatochlora arctica and butterflies such as Colias palaeno and Boloria aquilonaris. Drainage, peat cutting and afforestation stop the peat forming process and lead first to the degraded stage of 7120; separation from fen and transition mire vegetation rests on the exclusively rain fed water supply.

Raised bogs in which the natural hydrology of the peat body has been disrupted, usually by drainage, drainage related land use or peat cutting, leading to surface desiccation and a shift in species composition. The vegetation still carries most species typical of active raised bog 7110, such as Sphagnum and Eriophorum vaginatum, but their relative abundance has changed and birch, Betula pubescens, often establishes on the drier surface. The defining criterion is capacity for natural regeneration: sites qualify where the hydrology can realistically be restored and where appropriate rehabilitation offers a reasonable prospect of re-establishing peat forming vegetation within about thirty years. Sites dominated by bare peat, by agricultural grasses or crops, or where bog vegetation has been eliminated under a closed birch or pine canopy, no longer qualify. Distinguishing this type from active raised bog rests on the altered species balance and visible surface desiccation, not on the presence or absence of any single species.

Extensive bog landscapes on flat or gently sloping ground with poor surface drainage, confined to oceanic climates with very high rainfall, above all western and northern Britain and Ireland, with small outliers on the western seaboard of Scandinavia and in France, Portugal and Spain. Despite some lateral water movement the bogs are mostly ombrotrophic, with Sphagnum species such as S. papillosum, S. compactum, S. rubellum and S. tenellum playing a leading role alongside Calluna vulgaris, Eriophorum vaginatum, Molinia caerulea, Narthecium ossifragum and Trichophorum cespitosum. Two regional forms are recognised: hyperoceanic blanket bog of the western coastlands, locally with mucilaginous algal deposits, and blanket bog of higher ground and hills further inland. The extensive, undulating cover typically includes pools, flushes and terrestrial hummocks in the same complex, and supports breeding waders such as Pluvialis apricaria. Separation from raised bog rests on the sloping, blanket forming topography rather than the domed profile of a true raised bog.

Peat forming vegetation of oligotrophic to mesotrophic waters, intermediate between soligenous fens and ombrogenous bogs, comprising plant communities from swaying swards and floating carpets to true quaking mires. Dominants are medium and small sedges such as Carex lasiocarpa, C. diandra, C. rostrata and C. limosa, together with Sphagnum and brown moss carpets, Menyanthes trifoliata, Scheuchzeria palustris and, locally, the rare orchids Hammarbya paludosa and Liparis loeselii. In the boreal region the type also covers minerotrophic fens not part of a larger mire complex and small fens at the transition between open water and mineral soil. The vegetation belongs to the Scheuchzerietalia palustris and Caricetalia fuscae orders and is typically fringed by open water and amphibious communities. It is highly sensitive to drainage and to changes in the water level of the adjoining lake or pond, which shift it towards drier fen vegetation; separation from raised bog rests on its minerotrophic water supply, from open water on the peat forming floating or quaking mat.

Pioneer vegetation of open, wet peat and occasionally sand, low growing and often sparse, dominated by Rhynchospora alba and R. fusca together with Drosera intermedia, D. rotundifolia and Lycopodiella inundata. It colonizes bare, waterlogged peat surfaces exposed by erosion, cutting or seepage on blanket bogs and raised bogs, and also occurs naturally in frost or seep eroded patches of wet heaths and bogs and in the fluctuation zone of oligotrophic pools with sandy, slightly peaty ground. The white flowering heads of Rhynchospora alba together with the two sundew species are the surest field marks, since the vegetation stays open and never closes into a continuous sward. Because it depends on continuing surface disturbance, whether from natural frost and seep erosion or from historic peat cutting, it disappears once the surface stabilizes and drier bog vegetation closes in. It stands close to, and often borders, shallow bog hollows and transition mires, from which it is told apart by its pioneer, open character on bare peat rather than an established sward.

Cold, oxygen and mineral rich groundwater discharge sites of Fennoscandia, occurring either as true springs with a basin and adjacent outflow or as springfens where water seeps up through accumulated peat. They are fed by deep groundwater that keeps flowing through winter even when the land is frozen and snow covered, across the lowlands and uplands of Scandinavia. Recognition rests on a distinctive flora and a brown moss carpet: Cardamine amara, Chrysosplenium species, Carex paniculata and C. capillaris among the vascular plants, and Bryum pseudotriquetrum, Bryum weigelii, Philonotis species and Calliergon giganteum among the bryophytes; the invertebrate fauna is often highly specific to this cold water regime. The habitat depends entirely on the uninterrupted, unfrozen groundwater supply and is vulnerable to drainage or any lowering of the water table. It is related to, but distinguished from, the wider intermediate fen and soft water spring mire type by its northern, Fennoscandian range and year round flow.

Reed-like stands of Cladium mariscus, the great fen sedge, forming beds in the emergent zone of lakes, on fallow ground, or as a succession stage of extensively used wet meadows. The type occupies calcium rich, permanently or seasonally waterlogged ground in contact with Caricion davallianae fen vegetation or with other reed swamp communities of the Phragmition. In the field the tall, sharp edged leaves and dense, uniform growth of Cladium mariscus dominate the stand visually and are unmistakable; associated fen sedges and, on some coastal sites, the halophyte tolerant Kosteletzkya pentacarpos may accompany it. As a priority habitat it typically develops where open water silts up or where the management of wet meadows lapses, and it is lost through drainage, eutrophication, or the abandonment of the light cutting regime that once kept some stands productive without shading them out. It is separated from the calcareous fens of the Caricion davallianae by the dominance of tall Cladium mariscus over the low sedge and brown moss carpet that characterizes those fens.

Peat- or tufa-forming small sedge and brown moss mires fed by base rich, calcareous groundwater, with the water table at or close to the surface throughout the year. The type ranges from soligenous or topogenous mires of the European lowlands to alpine flushes, wherever groundwater maintains the base status the type needs. A brown moss carpet of Campylium stellatum, Palustriella commutata and Scorpidium revolvens accompanies small sedges such as Carex davalliana, C. lepidocarpa, C. hostiana and C. panicea, Eleocharis quinqueflora and Schoenus nigricans and S. ferrugineus, with Epipactis palustris, Primula farinosa and several Dactylorhiza orchids. It is among the most severely declined habitats in Europe, through drainage, eutrophication and the loss of light grazing or mowing that once kept competitors down; regionally it grades into Molinion wet grassland, and small stands occur in dune slacks or transition mires. It is separated from the Cladium fen (7210) by its low physiognomy rather than tall reed growth, and from acid poor fens by its calcareous water.

Low, open pioneer vegetation of small Carex and Juncus species colonizing gravelly, sandy or stony ground kept permanently cold and wet by meltwater, in moraines, at spring edges and along the margins of glacial torrents in the alpine and subalpine belts. It occupies neutral to slightly acid substrates in the Alps and neighbouring ranges and locally in northern Britain, and depends on a permanent or long lasting soil frost for its existence. Characteristic species include Carex atrofusca, C. bicolor, C. maritima, C. microglochin, Juncus triglumis, J. alpinoarticulatus and Kobresia simpliciuscula, growing as scattered, unstable patches on bare ground rather than as a closed sward. As a priority type it is maintained entirely by constant disturbance from moving icy water and repeated freeze-thaw cycles, which prevent peat accumulation and keep the vegetation permanently pioneer in character. It corresponds to the wider arctic-alpine rich fen vegetation but is narrower in range, restricted to the alpine and peri-Alpine mountains and their soil frost regime.

Mire complexes of the northern boreal and orohemiarctic zone in which peat mounds called palsas, containing a permanently or seasonally frozen core, rise two to four metres, exceptionally up to seven metres in Finland and Sweden, above the surrounding minerotrophic mire. The type occurs where the climate is slightly continental and the mean annual temperature stays below minus one degree, chiefly in northern Fennoscandia. The domed palsas themselves, with their sporadic permafrost, stand out clearly from the surrounding wet mire, which carries species such as Eriophorum russeolum, Carex saxatilis, Betula nana and Empetrum nigrum ssp. hermaphroditum together with lichens of the genera Cladonia and Cladina. As a priority type it depends wholly on the persistence of permafrost, and ongoing climate warming causes palsas to collapse and thaw, making it one of the most direct climate signals among the Annex I types. The surrounding non-permafrost mire is not itself part of the type; only the frozen peat mounds and their immediate vegetation belong to it.

Sparsely vegetated screes of shifting, coarse siliceous debris extending from the upper montane belt to the permanent snow line. Two related settings belong here: high alpine cryoclastic scree fields of variable grain size in the Alps and neighbouring ranges, and, further north and west, montane screes of western and central Europe, some of them of artificial origin from stone extraction. Alpine stands carry Androsace alpina, Oxyria digyna, Geum reptans, Ranunculus glacialis and Linaria alpina, while the lower, often fern rich stands hold Cryptogramma crispa and Athyrium distentifolium alongside bryophytes and lichens. The vegetation is kept open by continual downslope movement of the scree material; where movement slows, the sparse pioneer cover gives way to closed vegetation. It is separated from calcareous screes of the same altitudinal range (8120) by its siliceous, base poor substrate and correspondingly more acidophilous flora.

Screes of calcareous rock, calcshist or marl material extending from the montane to the alpine belt under cold climates, colonized by three related pioneer communities. The type occupies cold, unstable rock debris slopes of the Alps and neighbouring high ranges. The Drabion hoppeanae of calcshist screes carries Draba hoppeana and Saxifraga biflora, the Thlaspion rotundifolii of calcareous screes carries Thlaspi rotundifolium, Hutchinsia alpina and Papaver rhaeticum, and the Petasition paradoxi of marl screes carries Petasites paradoxus and Gypsophila repens. Vegetation cover stays sparse and open as long as the scree remains mobile, closing only once the slope stabilizes and finer soil accumulates. It is distinguished from the lower altitude Medio-European calcareous scree type (8160) by its higher, alpine to subalpine position, and from siliceous scree (8110) by its calcareous substrate and base loving flora.

Screes of warm, sun exposed slopes comprising several related sub-types across the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean mountains and locally warm sites of central Europe. The type occupies calcareous or siliceous coarse debris on unstabilized, sunny slopes from Mediterranean lowlands to alpine altitudes. Peri-Alpine stands carry Achnatherum calamagrostis and Gymnocarpium robertianum, Provencal screes hold Centranthus ruber and Crucianella latifolia, Pyrenean stands carry Iberis spathulata and Saxifraga praetermissa, and the screes of the Sierra Nevada are rich in local endemics. As with other scree types, the vegetation depends on continued substrate mobility from rockfall and frost action; once the slope stabilizes, scrub and woodland encroach. It is explicitly distinguished in the interpretation manual from the priority Medio-European calcareous scree (8160), the two occupying related but distinct geographic and climatic ranges that are easily confused in the field.

Limestone and serpentine screes of the Balkan peninsula and the larger eastern Mediterranean islands, carrying vegetation of the Drypidetalia spinosae. The limestone sub-type occupies higher Greek mountains such as Pindus, Olympus, Parnassus and Taygetos, a rarer serpentine form is restricted to outcrops of the Pindus, and the Illyrian screes occupy the alpine to montane belts of the Dinaric, Pelagonian and Moesian ranges together with coastal Croatia and Montenegro. Drypis spinosa and Aethionema saxatile mark the Greek limestone screes, Campanula hawkinsoniana and Silene haussknechtii the serpentine form, and Peltaria alliacea the Illyrian screes. As with other scree types, openness of the vegetation depends on continuing substrate movement from rockfall and frost action. The serpentine sub-type is floristically distinct and far more restricted than the surrounding limestone scree, and the whole type is separated from the Alpine calcareous scree types by its Balkan and eastern Mediterranean range.

Siliceous screes of the hills of western and central Europe, often impoverished derivatives of alpine scree vegetation and frequently originating from quarrying. The type occupies upland siliceous slopes below the true montane belt. Epilobium collinum, Galeopsis segetum, Senecio viscosus and Anarrhinum bellidifolium accompany a moss and lichen rich cover, with Cryptogramma crispa establishing where fern growth is possible. Many stands are of secondary, quarry origin, and the vegetation stays thin and open as long as the surface remains mobile. It is separated from the higher altitude siliceous scree of the montane to snow levels (8110) by its lower, hill country position and its floristically poorer, often more artificial character.

Calcareous or marly screes of the hill and montane belt, locally extending into the subalpine and alpine, often on dry, warm sites, with vegetation of the Stipetalia calamagrostis. The type occupies the hill and mountain country of central Europe. Achnatherum calamagrostis, Gymnocarpium robertianum, Galeopsis angustifolia, Petasites paradoxus and Rumex scutatus typify the open scree cover. As a priority type it is kept open by continued rockfall and downslope creep; once the scree stabilizes, shrubs and eventually forest colonize it. The interpretation manual explicitly separates this priority type from the non-priority Western Mediterranean and thermophilous scree (8130), the two occupying related but geographically and climatically distinct ranges.

Vegetation rooted in the fissures of limestone cliffs, ranging from the Mediterranean basin through the Euro-Siberian region to alpine altitudes and belonging chiefly to the Potentilletalia caulescentis and Asplenietalia glandulosi. It occupies vertical or steeply inclined calcareous rock faces at all altitudes; two broad levels are distinguished, a thermo- and meso-Mediterranean form with Campanula versicolor and C. rupestris, and a montane to oro-Mediterranean form that includes the Balkan endemic genus Ramonda. Ferns and hemicryptophytes rooted in the crevices, such as Asplenium species, Cystopteris fragilis and Draba aizoides in shaded and xerophilous variants respectively, give the type great regional diversity through many locally endemic species. The habitat is stable and slowly changing, governed by rock chemistry and exposure rather than management, and little threatened except by quarrying or climbing pressure. It is separated from siliceous chasmophytic vegetation (8220) purely by the calcareous rock chemistry and calcicole flora.

Vegetation of the fissures of siliceous inland cliffs, differentiated into numerous regional sub-types across Europe. The type occupies siliceous rock faces from the Pyrenees and Alps through the Hercynian massifs to the Iberian mountain ranges. High alpine stands carry Androsace vandellii, Saxifraga retusa and Eritrichium nanum, Hercynian serpentine cliffs their own specialists such as Asplenium cuneifolium and A. adulterinum, and lowland oceanic stands Asplenium septentrionale and A. billotii. The habitat is as stable as its calcareous counterpart, governed by rock chemistry, exposure and slow weathering rather than by management. It is distinguished from calcareous chasmophytic vegetation (8210) by the siliceous, often serpentine substrate and its distinct, more acidophilous or serpentine tolerant flora; serpentine stands in particular carry a highly specific set of Asplenium species not found on ordinary silicate rock.

Open pioneer vegetation of shallow soils on siliceous rock surfaces, dominated by succulent Crassulaceae, mosses and lichens under drought stress. The type occupies rock outcrops and thin, skeletal soils on silicate bedrock, generally at low to moderate altitude. The Sedo-Scleranthion carries Sempervivum species, Sedum annuum and Silene rupestris, the Sedo albi-Veronicion dillenii carries Veronica dillenii, V. verna and Gagea species, and both alliances share Sedum acre, S. album and Scleranthus perennis alongside the mosses Polytrichum piliferum and Ceratodon purpureus. It is an inherently open, drought limited pioneer community that persists as long as the soil stays too thin and dry for closed grassland to establish. It grades into the broader, more general EUNIS category of cryptogam and annual dominated vegetation on siliceous rock outcrops, of which it forms only the Sedo-Scleranthion and Sedo albi-Veronicion component.

Karst landscapes of regular limestone blocks, the clints, separated by a network of vertical fissures, the grykes, with the rock surface largely bare of overlying soil. The type occupies glacially eroded and weathered limestone terraces, notably in Britain and Ireland and, in a more continental form with larger blocks and smaller cracks, in Sweden. The fissures hold a cool, humid microclimate with shade tolerant species such as Geranium robertianum and Ceterach officinarum, thin soil pockets carry Mesobromion grassland, and Dryas octopetala survives as prostrate growth under grazing and wind exposure; Irish stands additionally carry Gentiana verna and, in the Burren, the orchid Neotinea maculata. As a priority type it is maintained as a fine scale mosaic by grazing, which keeps woody encroachment in check; abandonment allows scrub such as Corylo-Fraxinetum to spread and soil to accumulate. Its mosaic character means the pavement grades locally into calcareous grassland, scrub and woodland, from which it is set apart by the dominant bare rock and fissure structure.

Underground cavities not accessible to visitors, including their water bodies and streams, that host specialized or highly endemic species or are important for the conservation of Annex II species such as bats and amphibians. The type occurs wherever karst regions across Europe have developed cave systems. Vegetation is limited to mosses such as Schistostega pennata and algal carpets near the entrance; the diagnostic value lies chiefly in the fauna, a highly endemic assemblage of cave dwelling invertebrates, notably beetles of the Bathysciinae and Trechinae, and, in cave waters, crustaceans including Isopoda, Amphipoda and Copepoda, together with rare amphibians such as Proteus anguinus and Speleomantes species; caves also serve as hibernation sites for most European bat species. The type is defined by the constancy of the underground environment rather than by successional change, and disturbance from visitors threatens the specialized fauna. It is restricted to caves closed to public access, since visited caves face different pressures.

Sparsely vegetated to entirely bare surfaces on the products of recent volcanic activity: lava flows, ash and lapilli fields, fumarole vents and the hollow basaltic tubes left by cooling lava. Known from the active volcanoes of Tenerife, La Palma and Etna. Cover ranges from absent to extremely open; lichens such as Stereocaulon vesubianum and a few vascular pioneers are the first colonisers of bare rock. Above roughly 3000 metres on Teide a distinct summit community of Viola cheiranthifolia with Silene nocteolens and Argyranthemum teneriffae occupies the youngest ash; a separate assemblage occupies the Etna summit. The lava tube of La Corona on Lanzarote shelters a lightless fauna unrelated to surface vegetation, with the endemic decapod Munidopsis polymorpha and several Speleonectes crustaceans. Fumaroles carry their own sparse, heat adapted communities. The type is defined by substrate age, not by a characteristic plant cover; once soil has formed, closed vegetation and the summital hedgehog heaths of the Canaries belong to separate, later successional types.

Permanent ice bodies of the high mountains and the far north: true glaciers fed by compacted snow and flowing slowly downslope under gravity, and rock glaciers where ice is mixed with coarse debris. Forms range from unconstrained ice caps and ice sheets in arctic settings to topography bound cirque, valley and piedmont glaciers in the great mountain ranges, down to small, short lived glacierets fed by avalanche snow or ice deposition in cold karst dolines. Vegetation is absent by definition; the type is delimited by permanence of ice rather than by any biota. Persistent snow patches that do not flow belong to the separate snow pack type, and once a glacier has retreated its bare moraine is a distinct, ice free type until revegetation begins. Distinguishing a true glacier from a rock glacier in the field rests on the proportion of visible ice to surface debris cover.

Natural old growth forests of the boreal zone, dominated according to site by Pinus sylvestris, Picea abies or a mixture of both with birch, and the young stands that develop naturally after fire. Old stands carry a large volume of dead wood, a wide range of tree ages and a stable understorey microclimate, features that intensive forestry has removed almost everywhere in Fennoscandia; today they survive mainly in eastern and northern Finland and northern Sweden. Field and ground layers are dominated by Vaccinium myrtillus, V. vitis-idaea and Empetrum nigrum over the mosses Pleurozium schreberi and Hylocomium splendens and Cladonia lichens. Deadwood specialists give the type away: the lichen Lobaria pulmonaria, polypore fungi such as Fomitopsis populicola, the beetle Tragosoma depsarium and birds like the three toed woodpecker Picoides tridactylus and the Siberian jay Perisoreus infaustus. Fire suppression and forestry have made old growth stands and their post fire successions extremely rare, so present day fragments are refuges for red listed species rather than a representative sample of former boreal forest.

Old, natural hemiboreal broad leaved forests forming the transition between the western taiga and the nemoral forests of Fennoscandia, dominated by Quercus robur, Ulmus glabra, Fraxinus excelsior, Tilia cordata or Acer platanoides. Stands carry a long continuity of woodland cover and a large volume of dead wood, conditions that support an exceptionally rich flora of epiphytic lichens and bryophytes: Lobaria pulmonaria, the moss Antitrichia curtipendula, Homalia trichomanoides and Orthotrichum and Porella species on trunks and branches. Many stands were formerly grazed or mown, which kept the canopy open without removing the broad leaved character. In the field the type is told from ordinary hemiboreal mixed forest by this epiphyte load and by the long absence of clear felling, since the epiphytes need decades to centuries to build up. The wider EUNIS Carpinus and Quercus mesic deciduous forest covers much more ground than this narrowly defined, epiphyte rich Fennoscandian type.

Natural woodland forming on the land upheaval coasts of the Baltic Sea, where the retreating shoreline continually exposes new ground for primary succession. Soil horizons are poorly developed, in contrast to the podsols otherwise typical of boreal forest, and the vegetation runs a full successional sequence from shore grassland through pioneer thickets to climax forest or, on wetter ground, through willow swamp and forest swamp to mire. The youngest stands nearest the sea are herb rich deciduous thickets and swamps dominated by alder and birch with abundant willows in the shrub layer and a grassy field layer; further inland, as marine influence fades and soils grow poorer, pine and often spruce take over the canopy with dwarf shrubs beneath and mosses or lichens on the ground. Because every stand is a snapshot of an ongoing succession rather than a stable endpoint, delimitation in the field rests on position relative to the retreating shoreline and on stage of succession, not on a single characteristic tree layer.

Mountain birch forests of the Scandinavian subalpine belt and of isolated northern Fennoscandian fells and subarctic uplands, dominated by Betula pubescens ssp. czerepanovii, often as the sole tree species at the transition to open tundra. Two ecological poles are recognised: poor types on nutrient weak ground, with a field layer of Empetrum hermaphroditum, Vaccinium myrtillus and lichens of the genus Cladonia over mosses such as Pleurozium schreberi and Hylocomium splendens, and rich types on more fertile, often base influenced soils, with tall herbs including Geranium sylvaticum, Trollius europaeus, Cicerbita alpina and Aconitum lycoctonum. The type occupies the belt directly below the treeless fell tops and directly above the boreal conifer forest, so its upper and lower limits, not a single indicator species, are what separate it from alpine heath above and taiga birch or pine forest below.

Herb rich spruce forests of Fennoscandia, developed on brown forest soils with mull humus in low lying ground, ravines and slopes with fine sediment and a favourable water regime. Succession leads towards dominance of Picea abies, though broad leaved trees often remain a significant admixture. The type is distinctly layered, with an uneven bryophyte carpet, a field layer dominated by tall herbs and ferns, and well developed shrub and tree layers; dry, mesic and moist grass herb forest are the main variants, the composition shifting considerably between northern, southern and western Fennoscandia. Diagnostic herbs include Actaea spicata, Paris quadrifolia, Matteuccia struthiopteris and the orchids Cypripedium calceolus and Calypso bulbosa; where groundwater runs close to the surface, a wet forest flora with Epipogium aphyllum can appear. The herb rich, fern dominated field layer is what separates this type in the field from the dwarf shrub and lichen dominated dark taiga.

Coniferous forest growing on, or immediately adjoining, glaciofluvial eskers, the sorted gravel and sand ridges left by meltwater beneath retreating ice sheets, which can rise more than twenty metres above the surrounding land. Pinus sylvestris typically holds the exposed ridge crest, Picea abies the slopes, with some admixture of broad leaved trees. Aspect and slope steepness govern a microclimate that varies far more sharply than on the flat forest around, so sun exposed slopes carry a comparatively species rich flora with numerous legumes and even a few eastern steppe elements, among them Astragalus alpinus, Oxytropis campestris, Anthyllis vulneraria subsp. fennica and the pasque flowers Pulsatilla patens and P. vernalis, alongside Dianthus arenarius. In the field the esker landform itself, not the tree canopy, is the identifying feature, since the same Pinus sylvestris stands on flat ground belong to ordinary temperate or light taiga pine forest.

Open landscape mosaic of scattered trees or small copses over grassland, kept in this state by a long continuity of grazing rather than by any single soil condition. The tree layer is either broad leaved, most often Quercus robur, Fraxinus excelsior, Tilia cordata, Betula species or Alnus incana, or coniferous with Picea abies or Pinus sylvestris; in Sweden old, large, veteran oaks are a particular feature, their bark and dead or decaying wood carrying a rich assemblage of threatened lichens, fungi and invertebrates. In Finland the type also includes deciduous forest that developed after historical slash and burn cultivation. Regional variation is considerable, from birch, pine or alder dominated pastures in the boreal zone to oak, ash and hazel dominated forms in the hemiboreal south. Herb layer indicators such as Antennaria dioica, Campanula persicifolia and Succisa pratensis point to the sustained grazing that the type depends on; without it, closed forest replaces the pasture mosaic within a few decades.

Deciduous swamp forest under permanent influence of surface water, usually flooded every year, wet or moist and with some peat formation, though the peat layer stays thin. Fraxinus excelsior in the hemiboreal zone and Alnus glutinosa, reaching the middle boreal zone, are the characteristic trees, joined by Alnus incana, Betula pubescens and willows. A mosaic of small hummocks around the tree bases set against dominant flooded surfaces is typical of the structure. The type is most frequent in the southwestern Finnish archipelago and other Finnish coastal areas, rare inland in Finland but common throughout Sweden. Diagnostic herbs of the flooded ground include Carex elongata, C. diandra, Calla palustris, Thelypteris palustris and Lysimachia thyrsiflora over mosses such as Calliergon cordifolium. In the field the permanently wet, hummocky ground and the alder or ash canopy separate the type from drier broad leaved forest and from open fen without tree cover.

Acidophilous beech forest of the medio-European lowlands and hills, dominated by Fagus sylvatica alone at lower altitude and, in the higher mountains, joined by Abies alba or by both Abies alba and Picea abies. Soils are acid, and the field layer reflects it: Luzula luzuloides, Deschampsia flexuosa, Calamagrostis villosa, Vaccinium myrtillus and Pteridium aquilinum over the moss Polytrichum formosum, a sparse and low diversity layer compared with the beech forests on richer soil. Two altitudinal forms are distinguished, a collinar form of the lesser Hercynian ranges and the Alpine periphery often mixed with Quercus petraea, and a montane to high montane form of the greater Hercynian ranges, the Alps and the Carpathians. Delimitation from the neutrophilous beech forests of 9130 and 9140 rests on this acid, species poor field layer; where fir or spruce becomes co-dominant in the higher stands, the boundary to montane conifer forest is drawn by canopy composition rather than by the herb layer, which changes little.

Acidophilous beech forest of the Atlantic lowlands to montane belt, distinguished from other acid beech forest by Ilex aquifolium and, in the most oceanic areas, also Taxus baccata in the shrub layer. Soils are acid brown earths, leaching or tending towards podsol, with moder to dysmoder humus, under a humid Atlantic climate. Three varieties are recognised: subatlantic beech oak forest of the plains and hills with Ilex aquifolium; hyperatlantic beech oak forest of the same belt with both Ilex and Taxus and an epiphyte rich canopy; and montane pure beech or acidophilous beech fir forest with Ilex confined to the field layer. Companion species include Ruscus aculeatus, Deschampsia flexuosa, Vaccinium myrtillus, Teucrium scorodonia and Holcus mollis. In the field the presence of Ilex, and locally Taxus, in the understorey is what separates this type from the otherwise similar Luzulo-Fagetum of 9110, which lacks both.

Beech forest of neutral to near neutral soils with mild mull humus, spanning the medio-European and Atlantic domains of western and central Europe, dominated by Fagus sylvatica alone or, in the higher mountains, together with Abies alba or Picea abies. The herb layer is markedly richer and denser than in the acid beech forests of 9110 and 9120, with a strong presence of Anemone nemorosa, Lamium galeobdolon, Galium odoratum, Melica uniflora and, in the mountains, Dentaria species. Regional forms include a collinar type of the Hercynian arc and its surroundings, an Atlantic type with Hyacinthoides non-scripta in southern England and adjoining France, a montane type of the Jura, the Alps and the western Carpathians, a lime rich Bohemian form, and a Pannonic form on the plain's western margin. In the field, the abundant spring geophytes and the mull rather than moder humus separate this type from the acid beech forests, while a montane conifer admixture marks the transition towards 9140 and 9150.

Beech woodland near the upper tree limit in low mountains with oceanic climate in western Europe and the central and northern parts of central Europe, formed of low, low branching Fagus sylvatica with a strong admixture of Acer pseudoplatanus. The herb layer resembles that of the neutrophilous beech forests of 9130 or, locally, the acidophilous forests of 9110, but is enriched with elements of the adjoining open subalpine grassland, including Rumex arifolius. Stands are naturally stunted and open canopied because of exposure and a short growing season rather than through any land use. In the field the position at the tree limit, the low, crooked growth form and the abundance of sycamore are what separate this type from the closed, tall beech forest of the montane belt below it, and from treeless subalpine grassland immediately above.

Xerothermophilous beech forest on calcareous, often shallow soils of steep slopes in the medio-European and Atlantic domains of western and central Europe. Ligustrum vulgare and Berberis vulgaris typically enrich the shrub layer, and Buxus sempervirens can locally dominate it, while the herb layer carries sedges (Carex digitata, C. flacca, C. montana, C. alba), the grasses Sesleria albicans and Brachypodium pinnatum, and orchids of the genus Cephalanthera together with Neottia nidus-avis, Epipactis leptochila and E. microphylla, elements that spill over from the adjoining thermophilous oak woodland. A dry slope form on reduced water availability is the main expression in central Europe; a related xerophile beech form occurs on superficially dry limestone in the Cordillera Cantabrica of northwestern Iberia. In the field this rich, orchid and sedge dominated undergrowth on shallow rendzina like soil separates the type from the herb poor beech forest on deep neutral soil.

Oak or oak hornbeam forest of hydromorphic soils or ground with a permanently high water table, occupying valley bottoms, depressions and the fringes of riparian forest on silty, clayey colluvium or on weathered material rich in bases. Quercus robur dominates alone or with Quercus petraea, and mixed stands add Carpinus betulus and Tilia cordata, over a field layer of Stellaria holostea, Carex brizoides, Poa chaixii and Potentilla sterilis. Hyacinthoides non-scripta, characteristic of the Atlantic oak hornbeam forests further west, is absent or only rare here. Distribution runs through the sub-Atlantic and medio-European part of the Carpinion betuli range. In the field, the wet or seasonally waterlogged ground and the near absence of bluebell separate this type from the drier, better drained oak hornbeam forest of 9170 and from true alluvial forest closer to open water.

Oak hornbeam forest of the subcontinental climate zone within the range of Fagus sylvatica, dominated by Quercus petraea with Carpinus betulus, together with related lime oak forest further east, beyond the beech range, under a fully continental climate. Companion species in the western form include Sorbus torminalis, S. domestica, Acer campestre, Ligustrum vulgare and Convallaria majalis over sedges such as Carex montana and C. umbrosa; the eastern form adds Tilia cordata and Acer platanoides to the oak hornbeam canopy. Both forms occupy better drained, drier ground than the hydromorphic oak hornbeam forest of 9160, and lack the mull rich, spring geophyte dominated herb layer of the neutrophilous beech forests of 9130. In the field, the combination of Quercus petraea and Carpinus betulus on freely draining, subcontinental to continental sites is what separates this type from both.

Mixed forests of secondary tree species, Acer pseudoplatanus, Fraxinus excelsior, Ulmus glabra and Tilia cordata, on coarse scree, steep rocky slopes and colluvial deposits, mainly on calcareous but also siliceous substrates. Two sub-alliances are distinguished: the cool, humid Lunario-Acerenion, dominated by Acer pseudoplatanus, and the drier, warmer Tilio-Acerenion of screes, dominated by Tilia cordata and T. platyphyllos. Sites are steep and unstable, with constant substrate movement that keeps competition from beech and other zonal trees low. The herb layer carries Lunaria rediviva, Mercurialis perennis, Actaea spicata and Asplenium scolopendrium, with Lamium galeobdolon and Galium odoratum on more stable ground. The type occupies small, topographically fixed patches and changes little over time; threats come from quarrying and slope stabilisation rather than succession. It is separated from oak-hornbeam forests of the Carpinion by its restriction to scree and steep rocky terrain, not level ground.

Old, structurally simple oak woods dominated by Quercus robur, often with Betula pendula and B. pubescens and sparse Sorbus aucuparia and Populus tremula, on very nutrient-poor, sandy or morainic soils, podsolized or locally waterlogged, of the North European and Baltic lowland plains. The shrub layer is poorly developed, with Frangula alnus its main component; the ground layer is formed by Deschampsia flexuosa and other acid-soil grasses, sometimes Molinia caerulea, often overgrown by bracken. Stands correspond to Querco-Betuletum, Molino-Quercetum and Trientalo-Quercetum roboris in the north, and to Peucedano-Quercetum roboris further south on podzols with Quercus pyrenaica or hybrid oaks. Extreme nutrient poverty, not management, keeps these woods open and slow-growing; drainage and conifer plantation are the main threats. It is distinguished from richer oak-hornbeam and beech-oak woods by its acid, sandy substrate and poor ground flora.

Acidophilous woods of Quercus petraea with low, often multi-stemmed trees and a rich cover of ferns, mosses, lichens and evergreen shrubs, restricted to the British Isles. Two regional forms are recognised: the Irish sessile oak woods, especially rich in evergreen shrubs including Arbutus unedo, and the British sessile oak woods of western Britain, mainly Scotland, Wales, and northern and south-western England. Stands grow on acid, base-poor soils under the oceanic climate of the Atlantic seaboard, whose high, constant humidity favours an exceptionally dense bryophyte and fern layer. Ilex aquifolium and Blechnum spicant give the type its name, joined by Polytrichastrum formosum and Lonicera periclymenum. Grazing and coppicing have shaped most stands; excessive grazing pressure stops regeneration and thins the canopy. The type is set apart from continental acidophilous oak woods by its oceanic fern richness and from birch woods by the persistence of Quercus petraea as the main tree.

Thermophilous woods dominated by white oaks, Quercus pubescens and Q. virgiliana, forming azonal, submediterranean enclaves within the subcontinental zone of Quercion frainetto and Carpinion illyricum forests in south-eastern Europe. Two regional forms are distinguished: the Thracian white oak-oriental hornbeam woods of the Black Sea plains, the northern Thracian plain of Bulgaria and the Maritsa and Tundzha hills, and the Moesian white oak woods of the southern Dinarides, the Balkan Range and adjoining south-eastern Romania. Stands occupy warm, sheltered sites acting as thermal refugia within a cooler regional climate. The oaks are accompanied by Carpinus orientalis, Fraxinus ornus, Acer campestre or Tilia tomentosa, with submediterranean herbs such as Galium dasypodium and Paeonia peregrina. The type marks the northernmost extension of submediterranean white oak vegetation; clearing for pasture or arable use removes it outright, and it is separated from the surrounding, more mesic zonal forests by its thermophilous species set.

Thermophilous woods dominated by Fraxinus angustifolia, sometimes mixed with Quercus pubescens or Q. pyrenaica, occupying dry, non-alluvial and non-ravine sites, unlike the riverine ash woods with which the species is more usually associated. Two regional forms are known: the Sicilian narrow-leaved ash woods of western Sicily and the Iberian narrow-leaved ash woods of the Iberian peninsula. Stands grow on warm, often shallow soils away from watercourses, under submediterranean to mediterranean climate, so the ash trees draw water from groundwater rather than surface flooding. The type shares its thermophilous character with the submediterranean oak woods of the region but is set apart by the dominance of Fraxinus angustifolia. It is distinguished from the alluvial forests of 91F0 and the riparian ash-alder woods of 91E0 by its non-flooded position; grazing and clearing threaten the small, scattered remaining stands.

Forests of Abies alba, often mixed with Fagus sylvatica, Picea abies, Pinus sylvestris or Pinus nigra, forming a narrow belt on the northern slopes of the Rhodope, Balkan Range and Meso-Macedonian mountains, between the beech and coniferous zones. Stands grow on acidic, well-drained but moisture-rich soils. The field layer is heathy to herb-rich, with Prenanthes purpurea, Oxalis acetosella, Athyrium filix-femina and Galium odoratum, and Lonicera nigra and Polygonatum verticillatum in the fringe. Four regional forms are recognised, from the Rhodope and western Rhodope fir forests through the Moeso-Macedonian to the Balkan Range fir forests. The type occupies a thin transitional band, sensitive to any shift of the beech-conifer boundary through logging or climate change. It is separated from wider temperate mountain Abies forests by its restricted south-eastern range and from pure spruce forests by the dominance of Abies alba.

Relict, native pine forests of Pinus sylvestris var. scotica, endemic to the central and north-eastern Grampians and the northern and western Highlands of Scotland, with associated birch and juniper woods of northern character in the same area. Stands are mostly open, on acid, well-drained soils, with a ground layer rich in ericaceous dwarf shrubs and bryophytes, notably Hylocomium splendens and Pleurozium schreberi. Besides pine, the canopy includes Betula pubescens, B. pendula, Juniperus communis and Ilex aquifolium. Characteristic, often locally rare plants include Goodyera repens, Listera cordata, Linnaea borealis, Trientalis europaea and Moneses uniflora alongside abundant Deschampsia flexuosa. The forests are remnants of a once far larger native pinewood cover, reduced by historic felling and grazing that still suppresses regeneration. They are distinguished from planted stands by the endemic variety scotica and from other temperate Scots pine forests by their restriction to the Scottish Highlands.

Forests dominated by Pinus sylvestris on the southern slopes of the Rhodope, Rila, Pirin and Ossogovo mountains and the Balkan Range, extending to mountains of north-central and north-eastern Greece, on dry siliceous and calcareous soils. Stands are usually monodominant, occasionally with Pinus nigra subsp. pallasiana, Picea abies, Fagus sylvatica or Betula pendula. The shrub layer carries Juniperus communis, Vaccinium vitis-idaea and V. myrtillus; the herb layer is formed by Calamagrostis arundinacea, Brachypodium pinnatum, Sesleria latifolia and Pteridium aquilinum. Two regional forms are distinguished, the Rhodopide and the Balkan Range Scots pine forests. The type occupies dry, often steep and rocky montane sites where broadleaved trees cannot compete; wildfire and grazing have long shaped the open stand structure. It is separated from more western temperate Scots pine forests by its south-eastern, montane range and from black pine stands by the dominance of Pinus sylvestris.

Coniferous and broadleaved forests on permanently wet, nutrient-poor peat, with the water table always at or above ground level, so the substrate is more acidic and oligotrophic than an ordinary wet forest. Four regional forms are distinguished: birch bog woods with Betula pubescens, Scots pine mire woods, mountain pine bog woods with Pinus mugo, and mire spruce woods with Picea abies, the last also as minerotrophic strips along mire margins in the boreal region. The ground layer is built from Sphagnum species with Vaccinium oxycoccos, V. uliginosum, Eriophorum vaginatum and Carex rostrata; Frangula alnus and Molinia caerulea are frequent companions. The type depends entirely on an intact, stable water table; drainage for forestry closes the canopy and the peat vegetation disappears within decades. It is separated from open bogs and fens by the tree canopy, and from ordinary wet forests on mineral soil by its acid, Sphagnum-dominated peat substrate.

Riparian forests on heavy, alluvial soils that are flooded by the annual rise of the watercourse and well aerated at low water. Three forms are distinguished: ash and black alder along lowland and hill streams (Alno-Padion), grey alder along montane and submontane rivers of the Alps and northern Apennines (Alnion incanae), and gallery forests of tall Salix alba, S. fragilis and Populus nigra along the larger lowland rivers (Salicion albae). The herb layer is characteristically tall and lush, with Filipendula ulmaria, Urtica dioica, Carex spp., Angelica sylvestris and spring geophytes; nitrogen indicators reflect the regular sediment input rather than degradation. The type is tied to intact flooding dynamics: after damming or channel incision the stand persists for decades while its herb layer shifts towards that of a non-riparian forest, which is the usual reason for doubtful assignments in the field.

Hardwood floodplain forests of the outer, less frequently inundated parts of large river valleys and of depressions flooded mainly through a rising water table rather than direct overbank flow, developing on alluvial soils that may dry out between floods or stay moist. Depending on the local hydrology, the canopy is dominated by Quercus robur, Ulmus laevis and U. minor, or by Fraxinus excelsior or F. angustifolia, with Populus nigra and Alnus glutinosa as companions. The understorey is well developed, with Prunus padus, Humulus lupulus, Vitis vinifera subsp. sylvestris and Hedera helix, and a spring aspect of Corydalis solida and Gagea lutea. Stands depend on a less extreme flooding regime than the softwood forests they replace further from the channel; river regulation lets mesophilous trees invade. It is separated from softwood gallery forests of Salicion albae by higher, less flooded ground and from non-riparian oak-hornbeam forests by its liana-rich understorey.

Forests of Quercus petraea and Carpinus betulus on calcareous and siliceous substrates across the plains and low hills of south-eastern central Europe, with a shrub and herb layer dominated by subcontinental and submediterranean species. Stands occur in shaded, humid valleys and slopes with deep soils, but also on hilltops with shallow, oligotrophic ground. The herb layer includes Carex pilosa, Euphorbia amygdaloides, Dentaria bulbifera and Viola mirabilis, with Galanthus nivalis among the spring geophytes on richer soils, corresponding to Primulo veris-Carpinetum and Fraxino pannonici-Carpinetum. The type occupies a transitional position between central European oak-hornbeam forests and the Pannonian oak woods further south, reflecting the more continental, warmer regional climate; coppicing has shaped many stands. It is distinguished from wider central European Carpinion forests by its subcontinental herb layer, and from pure Pannonian oak woods by the co-dominance of Carpinus betulus.

Xerophilous oak woods dominated by Quercus pubescens, occupying the periphery and hills of the Pannonian plain on extremely dry, south-facing, shallow calcareous soils. Because of these harsh conditions the woods are often fragmentary, low-growing and locally reduced to scrub. The herb layer is species-rich and shares xerothermic species with the bordering dry grasslands, including Campanula bononiensis, Potentilla alba, Orchis purpurea and Dictamnus albus, with Cornus mas and Fraxinus ornus in the shrub layer; on better sites Tilia platyphyllos and Fraxinus excelsior can locally dominate. The type depends on the persistence of shallow, drought-prone calcareous ground; deeper soils allow taller, more mesic oak forest to develop instead. It is distinguished from wider submediterranean thermophilous oak woods by its restriction to the Pannonian basin, and from adjoining dry grasslands by its tree canopy.

Xerothermophilous oak woods of the plains of south-eastern Europe, developed on loess over chernozem soils under a strongly continental climate with a wide annual temperature range. The canopy is formed by Quercus robur, Q. cerris, Q. pedunculiflora and Q. pubescens, with Acer campestre, A. tataricum and Sorbus torminalis, corresponding to the Aceri tatarici-Quercion. The herb layer is notably rich in continental steppic elements and geophytes, including Tulipa biebersteiniana, Vincetoxicum hirundinaria and Buglossoides purpurocaerulea. The type marks the transition between closed deciduous forest and open steppe vegetation and is sensitive to grazing pressure and to ploughing of the chernozem soils it depends on, both of which have reduced it to scattered remnants. It is separated from the moister Pannonic and Illyrian oak-hornbeam forests by its steppic herb layer and loess substrate, and from open steppe by its tree canopy.

Woods overwhelmingly dominated by Taxus baccata, with Sorbus aria or a dense Mercurialis perennis ground layer, occupying dry valleys and scarps on chalk in south-east England, with very local outliers on the Durham magnesian limestone, around Morecambe Bay, and in the forest of Muckross near Killarney in Ireland. Stands grow on shallow, base-rich soils under a dense, evergreen canopy admitting little light, so Ilex aquifolium, Buxus sempervirens and shade-tolerant Mercurialis perennis are the main associates rather than a diverse field layer. The type often represents an arrested stage of succession or a senescent survival, since yew seedlings struggle under the deep shade of mature trees. It is distinguished from beech and oak-hornbeam woods with scattered yew by the overwhelming dominance of Taxus baccata, and its British distribution sets it apart from Mediterranean yew woods of the same alliance.

Beech forests of the Dinaric mountains and associated ranges and hills, with outliers reaching the south-eastern Alps, the south-western Carpathians and the mid-Pannonian hills, where they meet the medio-European beech forests of types 9130, 9140 and 9150. Fagus sylvatica, locally F. moesiaca, dominates the canopy, often with Abies alba, Ostrya carpinifolia, Quercus cerris and Tilia tomentosa. Species diversity is distinctly higher than in central European beech woods; the herb layer carries Aremonia agrimonioides, Cardamine trifolia, Helleborus niger subsp. niger, Omphalodes verna, Scopolia carniolica and Cyclamen purpurascens, and the Aremonio-Fagion forms a recognised centre of floristic richness among Europe's beech forests. The type occupies mainly montane and submontane slopes across a broad climatic transition zone, explaining its unusually varied flora. It is separated from the medio-European beech forests it borders by this richer, more thermophilous herb layer, not by canopy composition alone.

Forests of Quercus robur or Q. petraea, occasionally Q. cerris, together with Carpinus betulus, on calcareous and siliceous bedrock, mostly on deep, neutral to slightly acidic brown forest soils, across the south-eastern Alpine-Dinaric region and the western and central Balkans, extending north to Lake Balaton through hilly and submontane terrain and the plains of the Drava and Sava. The climate is more continental than in submediterranean regions and warmer than in central Europe, and species richness is markedly higher than in oak-hornbeam forests further north. The herb layer includes Erythronium dens-canis, Cyclamen purpurascens, Dentaria pentaphyllos and Primula vulgaris, with Acer tataricum and Tilia tomentosa contributing to the canopy. The type sits between the central European oak-hornbeam forests of 9170 and the more thermophilous Balkan oak woods. It is distinguished from the Pannonic oak woods of 91G0 by the greater share of Quercus robur and Q. petraea, and from beech forests by the co-dominance of Carpinus betulus.

Subcontinental, thermo-xerophilous forests of Quercus cerris, Q. petraea or Q. frainetto and related deciduous oaks, locally with Q. pedunculiflora or Q. virgiliana, distributed mainly between 250 and 600, locally 800 metres in the hills and plains of the Pannonian basin, western and southern Romania, the northern Balkan hill country and the supra-Mediterranean belt of continental north-eastern Greece and Anatolia, with Acer tataricum as a continental companion. The substrate varies widely, from limestone and andesite to loess, clay and sand, generally giving slightly acidic, deep brown soils. The herb layer is diverse, with Digitalis grandiflora, Veratrum nigrum, Asphodelus albus and Melittis melissophyllum, and Carpinus orientalis and Fraxinus ornus in the shrub layer. The type occupies a broad transitional zone between temperate and submediterranean oak forests and tolerates the drier conditions that exclude beech; clearing for pasture has long shaped its structure. It is separated from Illyrian and Pannonic oak-hornbeam forests by the absence or scarcity of Carpinus betulus.

Xerophilous mosaic of open Juniperus communis and Populus (P. alba, P. canescens, P. nigra) scrub with open to closed sand steppe grassland on inland dune sands of the Danube-Tisza interfluve in the Pannonian plain. The shrub layer carries Ligustrum vulgare, Rhamnus catharticus, Crataegus monogyna, Prunus spinosa, P. mahaleb, Euonymus verrucosus and Berberis vulgaris over open swards of Festuca vaginata, Koeleria glauca, Stipa joannis and Fumana procumbens, with orchids such as Epipactis bugacensis and Cephalanthera rubra. A true woodland herb layer is absent, giving the type more the character of semi-desert scrub than of steppe woodland and separating it from the denser thermophilous oak and oak-hornbeam forests of the surrounding lowland. Confined to a small area of extremely continental, drought-exposed sand, it depends on open, mobile or stabilising dune surfaces and is threatened by afforestation with introduced pines and by dune fixation.

Upland forests of Little Poland, chiefly the Holy Cross Mountains and sub-Carpathian hills, dominated by Abies alba alone or mixed with Picea abies, Pinus sylvestris and Quercus robur or Q. sessilis on mesotrophic, acid soils. The stand carries a rich fern and bryophyte layer, with Dryopteris austriaca, Athyrium filix-femina, Phegopteris connectilis, Lycopodium annotinum, Hylocomium splendens and Polytrichum formosum, alongside lowland forest herbs shared with the Tilio-Carpinetum, such as Galeobdolon luteum, Oxalis acetosella and Maianthemum bifolium. The type belongs to the wider group of temperate mountain silver fir forests but is set apart from Alpine and Carpathian Abies-Fagion stands by its restriction to the acid, mesotrophic uplands of Little Poland and by the admixture of lowland species. Continuity depends on natural fir regeneration under low-intensity management; conversion to spruce monoculture is the main threat.

Isolated calcicolous Scots pine forests confined to a few small enclaves of the western Carpathians (Strazov Mountains, Velka Fatra, Pieniny, inner-Carpathian basins) and the Erzgebirge, with related stands of the eastern Carpathians included in the same type. Stands grow on shallow, base-rich, rendzina-like soils and carry a xerothermic, partly continental undergrowth with Carex humilis, C. alba, Calamagrostis varia, Linum flavum and a set of western Carpathian endemics such as Pulsatilla slavica, Thymus carpathicus, Primula auricula subsp. hungarica, Campanula carpatica and Dianthus nitidus. Erica herbacea and Polygala chamaebuxus, characteristic of the wider group of montane calcicolous pine forests, are notably absent, separating the type from the more widespread Erico-Pinion stands of the Alps and Dinarides. The type occupies small, naturally open rock and scree sites and is vulnerable through its extremely restricted, fragmented distribution.

Pinus sylvestris woods on dolomite and dolomite rendzina of the Dinarides, developed within the zone of Illyrian beech forest and typically occupying somewhat higher elevations than the related dolomite black pine woods of the same mountains. The undergrowth is calcicolous and thermophilous, with Erica herbacea, Genista januensis, Galium lucidum, Buphthalmum salicifolium, Teucrium chamaedrys, Carex humilis, C. alba, Anthericum ramosum, Polygala chamaebuxus, Cyclamen purpurascens and orchids such as Epipactis atrorubens. Separation from the related black pine woods of the same dolomite substrates rests on the dominance of Pinus sylvestris and the somewhat higher, cooler position in the landscape; separation from the surrounding Illyrian beech forest rests on the open, light-demanding pine canopy tied to the shallow dolomite skeleton. The type persists on sites too shallow and dry for beech to close the canopy.

Fagus orientalis forests of the western Pontic range, the Strandzha-Istranca mountains and the eastern Balkan Range, distinguished by a markedly laurophyllous understorey of Euxinian affinity. Typical shrubs include Rhododendron ponticum, Daphne pontica, Laurocerasus officinalis (Prunus laurocerasus), Ilex colchica and Vaccinium arctostaphylos, with herbs such as Primula acaulis subsp. rubra, Trachystemon orientalis, Cyclamen coum and Epimedium pubigerum. In the eastern Balkan Range the laurophyllous shrubs drop out and Primula acaulis subsp. rubra and Trachystemon orientalis remain the most characteristic species, marking a recognisable regional variant within the type. Compared with the wider group of beech forests on base-rich to neutral soils, of which it forms a distinctive, geographically restricted southeastern outlier, this type is set apart by its Euxinian shrub and herb layer rather than by soil or altitude alone.

Natural, acidophilous Pinus sylvestris forests of the alliance Dicrano-Pinion on nutrient-poor inland sands of the northeastern Central European plains and hills and the middle to southern Sarmatic nemoral zone. Nutrient deficiency and drought stress on the sandy substrate keep the trees low-growing and the stand open, with a lichen-rich ground layer of Cladonia furcata, C. gracilis and C. rangiferina (as C. silvatica), Ptilidium ciliare and scattered Juniperus communis. The lichen dominance and low stature separate this type from the taller, more mesic Scots pine forests of the wider temperate continental group on richer or moister sands. Its distribution follows the driest, most oligotrophic dune and outwash sands, historically maintained by fire and low browsing pressure; afforestation practices that enrich or shade the ground layer eliminate the lichen carpet on which the type depends.

Xerophilous Scots pine woods of the Sarmatic region of western Eurasia and of areas with an extremely continental microclimate in northeastern Central and Eastern Europe, restricted at the western edge of the range to well-drained sites such as inland dunes and rock outcrops. The type gathers several regional associations, among them Peucedano-Pinetum, Koelerio glaucae-Pinetum sylvestris, Caragano-Pinetum and Corynephoro-Pinetum sylvestris, and carries many continental relict species alongside Pinus sylvestris, including Vaccinium myrtillus, Pyrola minor, Orthilia secunda, Chimaphila umbellata and the orchid Ophrys insectifera. Its steppic, extremely continental character and thin, well-drained soils separate it from the more mesic Dicrano-Pinion pine forests of the same broad temperate continental group. The type depends on open, undisturbed sandy or rocky ground and is threatened by afforestation, nutrient enrichment and closure of the canopy.

Fagus sylvatica forests, and their mixtures with Abies alba, Picea abies or Carpinus betulus, of the Romanian, Ukrainian and eastern Serbian Carpathians and the pre-Carpathian hills, belonging to the alliance Symphyto cordati-Fagion and developed on neutral to base-rich, occasionally acid-leaning substrates. Alongside the usual Fagetalia species the stands carry a set of Carpathian endemics and near-endemics, among them Symphytum cordatum, Cardamine glandulifera, Hepatica transsilvanica, Pulmonaria rubra, Leucanthemum waldsteinii and Ranunculus carpaticus. This endemic-rich herb layer is what separates the type from the wider group of beech forests on base-rich to neutral soils across the rest of temperate Europe, of which it forms the Carpathian, Symphytum-marked branch. Traditional selective forestry has generally maintained a near-natural structure; clear-felling and conversion to spruce are the principal threats.

Fagus sylvatica or Fagus x moesiaca forests of the Balkan Range, the southern Dinarides, the Moeso-Macedonian mountains, the Pelagonids and the Rhodopes, belonging to Doronico orientalis-Fagion moesiacae, with Abies alba and Picea abies joining beech at higher altitudes and latitudes.
