Despite lying at the southern edge of the beech range, the stands keep a pronounced Central European character, marked by frequent Acer pseudoplatanus, Quercus petraea, Fragaria vesca and Oxalis acetosella alongside Luzula luzuloides, Calamagrostis arundinacea, Galium odoratum, Cardamine bulbifera and Allium ursinum. This medio-European floristic signature, rather than any Euxinian or thermophilous element, is what distinguishes the type from other southeastern beech forests within the same broad group of stands on base-rich to acid soils. It occupies montane sites across a wide latitudinal range within its mountain systems.

A relict, extremely insular beech forest confined to the Macin Mountains, isolated within the steppe climate of the Romanian Dobrogea far from the main Carpathian beech range. The canopy mixes Fagus sylvatica with F. taurica, Tilia tomentosa, T. cordata, Carpinus betulus, Populus tremula and Ulmus glabra over an herb layer that combines Fagetalia species with southern European elements, including Potentilla micrantha, Scutellaria altissima, Carex pilosa, Carpesium cernuum and Melica uniflora. Its isolation inside a steppe-climate enclave, far outside the continuous beech belt, is what sets it apart within the wider group of beech forests on base-rich soils, rather than any single diagnostic species. The extremely small, disjunct range makes the type intrinsically vulnerable to drought, fire and any disturbance of the surrounding steppe matrix that shelters it.

Forests of Carpinus betulus with various oaks (Quercus robur, Q. petraea, Q. dalechampii, Q. cerris, Q. frainetto) on the flanks and piedmont of the eastern and southern Carpathians and the plateaux of western Ukraine, extending as azonal, often isolated stands into the Moesian Quercion frainetto zone, the eastern Pannonian and western Pontic steppe-woodland zone and the pre-Pontic hills of southeastern Europe. The herb layer combines typical Carpinion species such as Stellaria holostea, Carex pilosa, C. brevicollis and Dentaria bulbifera with an admixture of submediterranean Quercion frainetto elements and, in the east, Euxinian taxa such as Lathyrus hallersteinii and Aposeris foetida. This mixed, transitional composition separates it from the more uniform oak-hornbeam forests of the wider Carpinion group further west, of which it forms the southeastern, biogeographically enriched branch. Many stands are relict, azonal outliers in a landscape otherwise dominated by steppe woodland or thermophilous oak forest.

Tilia tomentosa dominated stands within mixed deciduous forests of southern Central Europe and the northern to middle Balkan Peninsula, mostly inside the range of Quercion frainetto but also locally within eastern Carpinion betuli forests, notably the Tilia tomentosa woods of the Carpinus betulus-Quercus petraea belt of Bulgaria. They occupy chiefly north-facing slopes of foothills on acidic, moisture-retentive soil and usually form near-monodominant stands, conspicuous when the canopy flowers. A rich spring aspect of geophytes, including Corydalis cava, C. solida, Scilla bifolia, Erythronium dens-canis and Ficaria verna, gives way in summer to a cover dominated by Carex sylvatica. Dominance by Tilia tomentosa on acid, moist, north-facing ground, rather than any single herb, distinguishes the type from the surrounding Quercion frainetto and Carpinion betuli forests within which it sits as a facies.

Thermophilous, highly fragmented beech forests of the Apennines, rich in endemics, with Taxus baccata and Ilex aquifolium in the understorey (Geranio nodosi-Fagion, Geranio striati-Fagion). Three regional forms are recognised: the Foresta Umbra of Monte Gargano, rich in Taxus baccata; silicicolous stands of the Aspromonte in Calabria with Taxus baccata, Populus tremula, Sorbus aucuparia and Betula pendula; and relict beech forests of the Madonie, Nebrodi and, very locally, the Peloritani, with Ilex aquifolium, Daphne laureola, Crataegus monogyna and Prunus spinosa. Compared with the wider group of beech forests on base-rich to neutral soils across temperate Europe, this type is set apart by its thermophilous, southern Italian and Sicilian distribution and by the constant presence of the evergreen understorey species Taxus baccata and Ilex aquifolium. Fragmentation and small population size of the endemic flora make individual stands especially vulnerable.

Beech forests of the Apennine hill level, on sites cooler than those carrying Taxus and Ilex, likewise highly fragmented and rich in endemics, here mixed with Abies alba or, in Sicily, the critically restricted Abies nebrodensis (Geranio nodosi-Fagion, Geranio striati-Fagion). The type includes relict beech forests of the Madonie, Nebrodi and, very locally, the Peloritani with Ilex aquifolium, Daphne laureola, Crataegus monogyna and Prunus spinosa, and the isolated beech forests of Mount Etna at the southern limit of the species' range. Admixture with silver fir, and on Sicily with the near-extinct Abies nebrodensis, distinguishes this type from the Taxus/Ilex-dominated Apennine beech forests and places it as a cooler, higher-altitude counterpart within the same endemic-rich Apennine beech group. Abies nebrodensis survives as one of Europe's rarest trees, giving the associated stands acute conservation weight.

Forests dominated by the marcescent Quercus pyrenaica, alone or with Q. robur, of the alliance Quercion robori-pyrenaicae, ranging from the supra- and meso-Mediterranean interior of Castile, the Cordillera Central and the Sierra Morena to the more oceanic, medio-European Cantabrian range, with outlying sub-Mediterranean stands in the Maestrazgo and the Sierra Nevada and further disjunct forests in south-western France. Regional composition shifts with climate: Cantabrian stands take on a more Central European character, drier interior stands carry Coronilla and other xerophytes, and the French outliers on poor sandy soils add Betula pendula, Deschampsia flexuosa, Molinia caerulea and Teucrium scorodonia. This broad, climatically graded distribution across Iberia and adjoining France, held together by the dominance of Q. pyrenaica, separates it from both the Atlantic acidophilous oak forests and the submediterranean thermophilous oak forests further east. Coppicing for firewood and charcoal has long shaped its stand structure.

Forests dominated by Quercus faginea, Q. canariensis or Q. afares across Iberia, ranging from the xero-mesophile Q. faginea woods of the Spanish Meseta and its bordering ranges to the humid, epiphyte-rich, relict Q. faginea forests of Portugal and the luxuriant, hyper-humid Q. canariensis forests of the Aljibe range and the Serrania de Ronda in extreme southern Spain, with further outliers in Catalonia and Mallorca. The humid southwestern Iberian forms are of outstanding biological importance and unique in Europe for combining a Mediterranean-latitude climate with Atlantic-level humidity, supporting a dense epiphyte and fern cover absent from the drier Meseta stands. This gradient from dry, deciduous Q. faginea woodland to humid, almost evergreen-appearing Q. canariensis forest, tied to a steep west-east humidity gradient across the peninsula, sets the type apart from the more uniform submediterranean thermophilous oak forests further east and north.

Supra-Mediterranean, occasionally meso-Mediterranean woods dominated by the semi-deciduous Quercus trojana or its allies (Quercetum trojanae), split into two disjunct regional groups: low Helleno-Balkanic stands, often mixed with junipers or maples, from Macedonia, Thrace and Thessaly north to Herzegovina, Montenegro, Albania and the Vardar valley, and taller, relict Apulian stands of Q. trojana with Q. pubescens and locally Q. ilex in the Murge of southern Italy. The wide geographic gap between the Balkan and Apulian populations, bridged only by the shared dominance of Q. trojana, is the defining feature separating this type from the broader submediterranean thermophilous oak forest group of which it forms a narrowly distributed, disjunct branch. The Apulian stands in particular survive only as small forest relics amid an otherwise cleared agricultural landscape.

Forests and old, established plantations dominated by Castanea sativa (sweet chestnut) in the supra Mediterranean and sub Mediterranean belts, with a semi natural undergrowth. Chestnut favours deep, well drained, acidic to neutral soils and avoids calcareous ground, which places most stands on siliceous substrates of hilly to submontane country. Long managed for fruit and for coppice wood, many stands are ancient plantations rather than primary forest, and their undergrowth often shares species with the acidophilous oak forests of the same regions, among them Quercus petraea and mosses such as Polytrichastrum formosum. Where management lapses, coppices grow into high forest, and on richer, moister ground the canopy tends to shift toward mixed deciduous woodland dominated by oak rather than chestnut.

Beech forests of the Greek mountains with a reduced medio European character and a high degree of endemism, assigned to the Fagion hellenicum. Fagus sylvatica typically grows together with the endemic fir Abies borisii-regis, and the field layer is characterised by Doronicum caucasicum, Galium laconicum, Lathyrus venetus and Helleborus cyclophyllus. Standort: montane belts of the Greek mainland, at altitudes where beech meets fir in mixed stands rather than pure beech woodland. Erkennung: the combination of beech with Abies borisii-regis and the named herb layer species distinguishes it from the wider Balkan and Aegean beech forests, which lack this fir and carry a more strongly medio European flora.

Forests of Fagus sylvatica or Fagus moesiaca that stand more thermophilous than the related supra Mediterranean and montane beech types, occupying the transition zone between the supra Mediterranean and the montane level. They are characterised by the presence of numerous species of the Quercion frainetto, so that Quercus frainetto figures alongside beech in the canopy or undergrowth rather than forming a pure oak forest. Standort: the warm, transitional altitudinal belt between typical beech forest above and thermophilous deciduous oak forest below. Abgrenzung: separated from ordinary supra Mediterranean and montane beech forest by this greater warmth demand and by the accompanying Quercion frainetto flora, and from lowland oak forest by the continued presence of beech in the canopy. The material available on this type is thin.

Montane forests of the Mediterranean basin dominated by native cypress, chiefly Cupressus sempervirens and, in North Africa, Cupressus atlantica or Cupressus dupreziana, assigned to the Acero-Cupression. Stands typically form an open canopy over a scrubby understorey and a herb rich field layer, on shallow, usually base rich soils in dry, rocky situations. The material available on this type is thin, limited to scattered montane occurrences across the Mediterranean rather than a single continuous range. Abgrenzung: separated from the wider Mediterranean juniper and cypress formations, which also include Juniperus species such as J. thurifera and J. excelsa, by the dominance of Cupressus itself rather than juniper.

Riparian forests of the Mediterranean and Black Sea basins, multi-layered and dominated by Salix alba or Salix fragilis, with tall poplars such as Populus alba usually forming the highest canopy layer. Stands can also include Ulmus, Alnus, Acer, Tamarix, Juglans regia, Quercus robur or Q. pedunculiflora and Fraxinus angustifolia, and where the tall poplars are sparse the canopy is instead dominated by these companion genera. Standort: periodically inundated terraces and gravel shoals of active floodplains, receiving regular deposits of nutrient rich alluvium. Erkennung: alliance Salicion albae, with a tall, nitrogen loving herb layer of Urtica dioica, Humulus lupulus, Rubus caesius, Phalaroides arundinacea, Glechoma hederacea and Calystegia sepium. Abgrenzung: the more strictly Mediterranean and Macaronesian riparian forests, which can include Platanus orientalis, form a related but broader group against which this type is set.

Distinctive, relict riparian formations of the thermo and meso Mediterranean zone confined to deep, steep sided valleys of southern Iberia. One form is an alder gallery with Rhododendron ponticum ssp. baeticum and Frangula alnus ssp. baetica in the shrub layer, Arisarum proboscideum in the field layer, and a rich, relict fern flora including Pteris incompleta, Diplazium caudatum and Culcita macrocarpa. A second, separate form is a birch gallery dominated by the extremely local endemic Betula parvibracteata, accompanied by Myrica gale, Frangula alnus, Salix atrocinerea, Galium broterianum and Scilla ramburei. Standort: canyon-like valley bottoms rather than open floodplains. Erkennung: the fern assemblage in particular points to a Tertiary relict flora surviving in a few humid refuges. Abgrenzung: distinguished from ordinary Mediterranean riparian forest of Populus, Salix and Platanus by this relict, highly localised, endemic-rich composition.

Mostly riparian woods of the eastern Mediterranean dominated by Platanus orientalis (oriental plane), assigned to the Platanion orientalis, with the Tertiary relict Liquidambar orientalis restricted to a single valley on Rhodes. Stands colonise poorly stabilised alluvial and gravel deposits along temporary rivers and, toward the southern edge of the range, the shaded bottoms of deep gorges; accompanying species include Salix alba, Alnus glutinosa, Celtis australis, Fraxinus ornus and Vitex agnus-castus, with a rich vernal layer of geophytes such as Cyclamen species and Arum italicum, and abundant ferns and mosses including Pteridium aquilinum. The main range runs through mainland Greece, from the Ionian coast and Pindus through Macedonia and Thrace to the Peloponnese, where gorge forests in the Taygetos reach 1300 metres, with outliers on Crete, Euboea and several Aegean islands. Relict, isolated occurrences also survive in deep gorges of south eastern Sicily, where plane is locally replaced or accompanied by Populus alba, Fraxinus angustifolia and Salix species. Erkennung: dominance of Platanus orientalis in the canopy, or, on Rhodes alone, of Liquidambar orientalis; confinement to gorges grows stricter toward the southern range limit.

Low, often open galleries and thickets built by Tamarix species together with Nerium oleander (oleander) and Vitex agnus-castus (chaste tree), on permanent or temporary watercourses and wetlands of the thermo Mediterranean zone and south western Iberia, reaching into the more hygromorphic sites of the adjoining Saharo Mediterranean and Saharo Sindian zones. In south western Iberia the type also carries Securinega tinctoria, Prunus lusitanica and Viburnum tinus. Related Tamarix smyrnensis stands of streamsides and coasts in the Pontic and steppic regions of western Eurasia belong here as well, but plain thickets built solely by Tamarix africana are excluded from the definition. Physiognomy: a shrubby, often open low ligneous formation rather than a closed forest. Erkennung: alliances such as Securinegion tinctoriae carry the more diverse south western Iberian form. Standort: it occupies the driest, most intermittently flooded riverbeds and streamsides, seasonally dry ground that separates it structurally from taller riparian gallery forest.

Open to closed woods dominated by Quercus brachyphylla, an oak of the Aegean region, often growing together with Quercus macrolepis (valonia oak) or Quercus ilex (holm oak). The material on this type is thin, limited to the bare statement of its dominant tree and its usual companions. Standort and general physiognomy correspond to the wider group of submediterranean thermophilous deciduous forests of the Aegean and Balkan area, a warm, transitional belt between temperate and fully Mediterranean conditions. Abgrenzung: separated from the other Aegean and Balkan oak woods primarily by the identity of the dominant oak, Quercus brachyphylla, rather than by a distinct physiognomy or ecology of its own.

Thermo Mediterranean, and in the Canary Islands thermo Canarian, evergreen sclerophyllous woodland dominated by wild olive Olea europaea ssp. sylvestris and carob Ceratonia siliqua, together with Pistacia lentiscus (mastic) and Myrtus communis; the Canarian counterpart is built by Olea europaea ssp. cerasiformis and Pistacia atlantica. Most stands present as an open, shrubby arborescent matorral, and only where the canopy closes and gains sufficient height does the vegetation count as forest proper. Erkennung: character species include Prasium majus, Smilax aspera, Arisarum vulgare and Asparagus acutifolius. Standort: drought prone lowlands and foothills of the thermo Mediterranean belt, on a range of substrates. Vorkommen: a near climax olive, carob and mastic forest survives on Djebel Ichkeul in northern Tunisia, with further relict stands in southern Andalusia, now nearly extinct, and on Menorca, Sardinia, Sicily, Calabria, Puglia and Crete. Because canopy closure is rare, most European examples persist only as degraded matorral rather than closed forest.

West Mediterranean forests on siliceous soil dominated by cork oak Quercus suber, generally more thermophilous and moisture demanding than related evergreen oak forests. Regional forms include meso Mediterranean stands of Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, France and north eastern Spain, assigned to the Quercion suberis and frequently degraded to arborescent matorral; south western Iberian stands, often mixed with Quercus faginea or Quercus canariensis, of the Quercion fagineo-suberis; a very localised outlier confined to the Sil and Mino valleys of Galicia within the Quercus pyrenaica belt; and isolated dune facies stands in the eastern Landes of Aquitaine. Standort: exclusively silicicolous ground, which separates it from base tolerant holm oak forest. Nutzung: long managed for cork harvest, many stands persist as open, semi natural woodland rather than closed high forest, and cutting or grazing readily degrades them to shrubby matorral.

Evergreen sclerophyllous forests dominated by Quercus ilex (holm oak) or, in Iberia, by the closely related Quercus rotundifolia, typically but not exclusively on base rich soils. Physiognomy varies with altitude: rich meso Mediterranean stands occupy the lowlands and penetrate locally into the thermo Mediterranean zone along ravines, supra Mediterranean stands at higher altitude mix with deciduous oaks, maples and Ostrya carpinifolia, and Quercus rotundifolia woodland of the Iberian interior is generally lower, drier and more open than true Quercus ilex forest. Erkennung: an understorey typically built from Arbutus unedo, Phillyrea angustifolia or P. latifolia, Rhamnus alaternus, Pistacia terebinthus, Rubia peregrina, Smilax aspera and Lonicera implexa or L. etrusca. Gefährdung: cutting and grazing readily reduce these forests to arborescent matorral or to open, dehesa-like woodland. Abgrenzung: distinguished from cork oak forest, which is confined to acid soils and demands more moisture.

Semi deciduous, often fairly open woods dominated by Quercus macrolepis (valonia oak, treated in EUNIS as Quercus ithaburensis subsp. macrolepis) of the meso Mediterranean zone, generally on shallow soil below about 700 metres. Vorkommen: continental Greece and its archipelagos and adjacent Albania, best developed in the Ionian islands and on Lesbos; more modified, grove like stands occur around the Gulf of Arta, in western Aetolia, the north western Peloponnese, Thessaly, Attica and Thrace; an isolated relict outlier survives at Salento in Apulia, southern Italy. Erkennung: canopy pure or mixed with other oaks including Quercus pubescens and Quercus ilex, alliance Quercion macrolepidis, with accompanying Rubia peregrina, Sorbus domestica, Phillyrea latifolia, Ruscus aculeatus, Pistacia terebinthus and Arbutus unedo. Nutzung: many stands are long managed groves rather than closed high forest.

Evergreen, laurel leaved cloud forest of the humid to hyper humid fog belt on the Macaronesian islands, among the most species rich and endemic rich forest types in Europe. The dominant trees vary by archipelago and include Laurus azorica, Ocotea foetens, Persea indica, Apollonias barbujana and Ilex canariensis, often over an understorey rich in ferns; genera such as Picconia, Semele and Ixanthus occur nowhere outside these forests. Standort: perhumid, fog bound, mostly north facing slopes of the mountain cloud belt, each archipelago carrying its own distinctive endemics. Best preserved on Madeira, where the type still covers a considerable area; on the Azores, low altitude coastal stands are largely degraded and invaded by the introduced Pittosporum undulatum, so the least disturbed examples are the hyper humid, high elevation forests, while Canarian laurel forest again differs floristically island to island. Abgrenzung: at higher, drier margins the laurel forest gives way to a lower, heathy woodland of tree heath Erica arborea and Ilex canariensis with strawberry tree Arbutus canariensis, a distinct, more open formation.

Sparse to locally dense palm groves formed by two European endemic palms, Phoenix theophrasti on Crete and adjoining south western Anatolia, and Phoenix canariensis in the Canary Islands, both often riparian or dependent on temporary water. Cretan groves occupy damp, sandy coastal valleys, the largest being the palm forest of Vai with a thick shrubby undergrowth rich in Nerium oleander, plus a handful of smaller coastal groves, notably on the south coast near Rethymno. Canarian groves grow at the bottom of barrancos and on alluvial soils below about 600 metres, dependent on brief temporary water tables built up by winter torrential flow, and so form azonal vegetation within the dry to arid infra and thermo Mediterranean belts; well known examples lie at Maspalomas and the Barranco de Tirajana on Gran Canaria, in the Valle Gran Rey on La Gomera, at Masca on Tenerife and at Brena Alta on La Palma. Erkennung: a sparse, open canopy of Phoenix, with accompanying species differing sharply between the two island groups, reflecting their independent, highly localised endemic status.

Stands dominated by tree sized, arborescent Ilex aquifolium (holly) of the supra Mediterranean level, on a range of substrates. The type is interpreted as a senescence stage: relict patches persist where the canopy of an evergreen oak forest carrying a Taxus and Ilex understorey, among others assigned to the Ilici-Quercetum ilicis, has died back or been removed, leaving holly as the dominant woody layer. Physiognomy: patches rather than extensive stands, occurring both within and outside closed forest. Erkennung: dominance of Ilex aquifolium in the tree or shrub layer; wider European holly patches outside this successional context also carry species such as Lonicera periclymenum and Quercus petraea. Abgrenzung: separated from ordinary evergreen oak forest with a holly understorey by the loss of the oak canopy, holly having taken over the dominant role.

Low forest and derived scrub dominated by the endemic golden oak Quercus alnifolia, confined to basic, eruptive rock of the Troodos range in Cyprus. Physiognomy ranges from arborescent, tree sized stands to degraded matorral derived from them by cutting and grazing. Erkennung: accompanying species include Acer sempervirens, Teucrium kotschyanum, Salvia cypria, Crepis fraasii and Sedum cyprium, several of them Cypriot endemics. Standort: basic eruptive substrate, a geologically narrow and geographically unique setting found nowhere else. Abgrenzung: distinguished from the wider Mediterranean evergreen Quercus forests by this strict endemism and by its confinement to a single mountain range.

Deciduous oak woodland dominated by Quercus infectoria, the potential natural vegetation of limestone and marly limestone slopes in the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus, between about 600 and 1100 metres. Associated trees and shrubs include Quercus brachyphylla, Arbutus andrachne, Acer syriacum, Fontanesia philliraeoides and Styrax officinalis, with Anagyris foetida, Cyclamen persicum and Eryngium falcatum in the field layer; the association is named Anagyro foetidae-Quercetum infectoriae. The type is endemic to Cyprus and confined to base-rich substrates within this altitudinal band. Once cleared or grazed, stands degrade first into evergreen Quercetalia ilicis maquis with Quercus coccifera subsp. pseudococcifera, and further into Cistus creticus phrygana; these degraded stages are read as part of the same series, not as a separate type. Separation from the island's evergreen oak formations rests on the deciduous character of Quercus infectoria itself.

Subalpine to montane coniferous forest dominated by Picea abies, occupying acidic, often oligotrophic soils across the temperate mountain systems of Europe: the outer, intermediate and inner Alps, the Hercynian ranges, the Carpathians and, as outlying stands at the southern edge of the species' range, the Apennines, the Dinarides and the Balkan Range. Trees are often stunted or narrowly columnar towards the tree line. Characteristic undergrowth includes Vaccinium myrtillus and V. vitis-idaea together with Oxalis acetosella, Prenanthes purpurea, Lonicera nigra, Melampyrum sylvaticum, Luzula sylvatica and Polygonatum verticillatum. In the inner Alpine valleys the type occupies sites climatically unfavourable to beech and fir, while peri-Alpine stands fill outlying altitudinal or edaphic enclaves within other montane forest types. Where silver fir (Abies alba) or beech become codominant on richer, less acidic soils, stands pass into fir or beech-fir forest, which is the usual boundary encountered in the field.

Subalpine, occasionally montane, coniferous forest of the central Alps and Carpathians dominated by Larix decidua or Pinus cembra, singly or mixed, sometimes with an admixture of Picea abies. On siliceous substrates of the eastern and central Alps the undergrowth is often species-poor, with Vaccinium myrtillus, Rhododendron ferrugineum, Calamagrostis villosa and Luzula albida; on calcareous ground the field layer is richer, with Erica herbacea, Polygala chamaebuxus, Rhododendron hirsutum and locally Pinus mugo. The larch's deciduous habit and the open, light canopy typical of both species let a rich herb and dwarf-shrub layer develop even at high stand density. Larix decidua sheds needles in autumn and colours conspicuously before doing so, a reliable field character against the evergreen spruce and pine forests it borders at the same altitude; Pinus cembra is told from Pinus uncinata of neighbouring forest types by its five-needle fascicles and large, wingless seeds.

Open subalpine and montane forest of mountain pine, Pinus uncinata, with a well-developed shrub layer, occurring on limestone, gypsum or siliceous substrates in the Alps, Jura and Pyrenees. On siliceous or decalcified soils of the western outer Alps, the Jura and Pyrenean north-facing slopes, the understorey is dominated by Rhododendron ferrugineum together with Vaccinium myrtillus, V. uliginosum and Calluna vulgaris; on the drier, south-facing or inner-Alpine sites Rhododendron ferrugineum is absent or rare, and the shrub layer instead carries Juniperus nana, J. hemisphaerica, Erica herbacea, Rhododendron hirsutum, Polygala chamaebuxus and Dryas octopetala. Arctostaphylos alpina, A. uva-ursi and Coronilla vaginalis recur across both forms. The priority status applies specifically to stands on gypsum or limestone. Separation from the calcicolous and siliceous larch and arolla pine forests of the same belt rests on the dominance of Pinus uncinata itself, recognised by its strongly asymmetric, hooked cone scales.

Relict silver fir (Abies alba) forest of the southern Apennines, occurring as scattered, small stands associated with beech woods of the Geranio versicolori-Fagion. The fir survives here at the southern, disjunct edge of its European range, in relic populations rather than as a continuous forest belt. Distinguishing the type in the field rests on the dominance or strong presence of Abies alba within an otherwise Fagus sylvatica-dominated matrix; it differs from the fir forests of Mediterranean mountains further south and east, which are built from separate, taxonomically distinct firs such as Abies pinsapo, A. cephalonica or A. borisii-regis, and from the northern acidophilous spruce-fir forests, which lack the Mediterranean beech associates.

Forest of the endemic Spanish fir, Abies pinsapo, restricted to a few mountain massifs of southern Spain in the supra- to meso-Mediterranean belt. Stands occur on calcareous ground and, locally, on ultrabasic serpentine outcrops, forming small, isolated populations rather than a continuous forest type. Abies pinsapo is recognised by its short, stiff, radially arranged needles, distinct from the flattened needles of Abies alba and the other Mediterranean mountain firs such as A. cephalonica and A. borisii-regis with which it shares the wider EUNIS grouping of Mediterranean mountain fir forest; each of these firs occupies its own, non-overlapping mountain range, so identification in the field is largely a matter of location.

Montane-Mediterranean pine forest on dolomitic substrate, often dense and closed, built from pines of the Pinus nigra group: Pinus nigra proper in the Alps, the Apennines and the western Balkans, Pinus dalmatica along the Dalmatian coast, Pinus salzmannii in Spain and the Causses, and the Corsican and Calabrian forms of Pinus laricio on granitic soils of Corsica and the Sila, Aspromonte and Etna massifs, with Pinus pallasiana replacing them in Greece and the Balkans. Stands are sometimes mixed with Pinus sylvestris and, more rarely, with Larix decidua or Pinus cembra. The Corsican laricio stands hold the entire European population of the Corsican nuthatch, Sitta whiteheadi. Because the constituent pines occupy separate, non-overlapping mountain ranges, field recognition rests mainly on locality and needle and cone characters of the local black pine taxon rather than on a shared undergrowth. The type is distinguished from the wider black pine and Scots pine forests of neighbouring, non-dolomitic substrates by its confinement to magnesium-rich, dolomitic ground.

Mediterranean and thermo-Atlantic pine forest of thermophilous, mostly light-demanding pines that typically occupy substitution or paraclimax stages of evergreen oak woodland (Quercetalia ilicis) or Ceratonio-Rhamnetalia scrub rather than forming permanent climax forest. The constituent species replace one another regionally: Pinus pinaster subsp. atlantica in south-western France and western Iberia, P. pinaster subsp. pinaster on siliceous ground of the western Mediterranean from Spain to Corsica and Sardinia, P. pinea (stone pine) around most southern European coasts, P. halepensis (Aleppo pine) on calcareous, drought-prone soils from Iberia to Greece, and P. brutia (Aegean pine) in Crete and the eastern Aegean. Long-established plantations of these pines within their natural range and with a similar understorey are counted as part of the type; recent, obviously artificial groves are not. All forms are markedly fire-prone and readily regenerate after burning, which distinguishes their dynamic from the evergreen oak forests they otherwise stand in for.

Forest of the endemic Canary pine, Pinus canariensis, on the dry montane slopes of Tenerife, La Palma, Gran Canaria and Hierro, roughly between 800 and 2000 metres. The undergrowth varies with exposure: sun-exposed slopes carry Cistus symphytifolius with Chamaecytisus proliferus, Adenocarpus foliolosus and Lotus campylocladus; dry, south-facing ground shows a scrubbier form with Cistus monspeliensis and Salvia canariensis; humid, fog-bound north-facing slopes are dominated by Erica arborea and Myrica faya under thick epiphytic lichens and mosses; near the upper limit Adenocarpus viscosus takes over, and on steep rocky ground Juniperus cedrus joins the pine. The type is the sole habitat of the Tenerife blue chaffinch, Fringilla teydea, and its fog-belt stands hold the Tenerife goldcrest, Regulus teneriffae. Pinus canariensis regenerates vigorously after fire, an adaptation no mainland European pine shares, and this fire ecology together with the endemic undergrowth separates the type from every other Mediterranean pine forest.

Medium-altitude forest dominated by tree junipers, distinct from the low arborescent juniper matorral of drier Mediterranean scrub. Several regionally distinct, taxonomically separate forms make up the type: Spanish juniper woods of Juniperus thurifera on calcareous, gypsiferous or locally siliceous ground of the Iberian Range, the Sierra de Guadarrama, the Cordillera Cantabrica, the Ebro basin and isolated valleys of Corsica and the south western Alps, often with Pinus sylvestris or P. salzmannii; Grecian juniper woods of J. excelsa in the mountains of northern Greece; stands of J. foetidissima and, very locally, J. drupacea on Mount Parnon; and, in Macaronesia, high-altitude J. cedrus on rocky slopes of Tenerife, La Palma, Gomera and Gran Canaria and endemic J. brevifolia forest in the Azores. Because these junipers do not overlap geographically, field recognition is chiefly a matter of locality and the size and colour of the seed cones. The type excludes low, shrubby juniper formations of comparable species, which are treated as matorral rather than forest.

Xerothermophilous forest and tall scrub of Tetraclinis articulata (Arbor-vitae), in Europe confined to a small area near Cartagena in south-eastern Spain, at the northern edge of a range otherwise centred in north-west Africa. Associated species include Chamaerops humilis, Periploca laevigata, Rhamnus lycioides, Lavandula dentata, Lithodora fruticosa and Teucrium carthaginense, with Brachypodium retusum and Asparagus albus in the field layer; the vegetation belongs to the Periplocion angustifoliae. Scrub formed by Tetraclinis articulata itself, not only closed forest, is counted as part of the type. Tetraclinis is recognised by its flattened, jointed, scale-leaved branchlets, similar at a glance to true cypress but structurally distinct, and by small, woody, star-shaped cones; within its very restricted European range no other conifer forest occupies the same warm, dry, low-elevation ground.

Local, often small-patch woodland dominated by yew, Taxus baccata, sometimes with holly (Ilex aquifolium) and box (Buxus sempervirens), on base-rich soils in scattered Mediterranean localities: mountain ranges of Corsica (Tenda, San Pedrone, Cap Corse), Sardinia (Catena del Marghine, Monte Limbara) and relict stands in northern and central Portugal (Serra do Gerês, Serra da Estrela). Two origins are recognised: a senescent phase of beech or beech-fir forest, in which yew forms clusters after the fall of the taller trees within an otherwise layered beech-yew stand, and residual, purely relict yew stands where the associated tall trees have already disappeared. Mercurialis perennis and Sorbus aria are frequent associates in the herb and shrub layers. Because yew tolerates deep shade and regenerates poorly in the open, its presence as the dominant tree, rather than as scattered individuals within beech forest, is what marks the type in the field.

Evergreen cedar forest endemic to the western summits of the Troodos range in Cyprus, dominated by the Cyprus cedar, Cedrus brevifolia, a species found nowhere else. Quercus alnifolia is a frequent associate in more open stands, with Arrhenatherum album and Galium peplidifolium in the herb layer; Cephalorrhynchus cypricus and Lindbergella sintensii are endemic associates restricted to the same massif. The type belongs to the wider group of Mediterranean mountain cedar forests that also includes Cedrus libani in Lebanon, Syria, Turkey and elsewhere in Cyprus, but Cedrus brevifolia is treated as a distinct species by most authors, smaller in stature and with shorter needles than C. libani, and its entire world range lies within this single mountain block, which alone is sufficient to identify the type in the field.

High-altitude coniferous forest of the southern Balkans, northern Greece and southern Italy, formed by two Balkan-endemic pines with distinct ecology: Pinus heldreichii (Bosnian pine), which forms open, often treeline stands on dry, stony or rocky, mostly base-rich soils with an undergrowth reduced to stripped grassland, and Pinus peuce (Macedonian pine), which occupies the subalpine belt of the high Balkan mountains south to Voras, Varnous and the Rhodope on mostly siliceous soils with a fuller undergrowth including Vaccinium myrtillus, Calamagrostis arundinacea, Luzula sylvatica and Geranium macrorrhizum. Picea abies, Pinus sylvestris and, near the tree line, Pinus mugo occur as associates in either form. Because the two pines differ so strongly in substrate preference and undergrowth, the type is best treated as two distinct forests sharing only their high-mountain, oro-Mediterranean position; needle number per fascicle (two in P. heldreichii, five in P. peuce) separates the trees themselves at a glance.
